The next day, being the 24th of the same month, we marched with the entire force through the whole village, the houses were burned, which they had in great numbers, and the entire village, which was extraordinarily well and beautifully built in the Indian manner, and moreover very full of clappus [a type of tree] and other various fruit trees, was set on fire, and the timber was spared as much as possible in order to lure them back to their village and bring them to obedience. This accomplished, we then marched to the village of Baccaluan [also written as Backaluan], which is located halfway between Mattauw and Sinckan, where we lodged that night. Being there on the 25th of the same month, we had the entire community of Baccaluan come together with the others, and through Dr. Junij explained to them in the Sinckan language why we had attacked Mattauw, and spared them in the hope that they would conduct themselves well (which they also promised to do), we marched to Sinckan, where we had one of the most notable and most culpable of the aforementioned murders, still in arms for the Company, beheaded by a Sinckan man as an example to others, and marched forth, the people having eaten somewhat, to Saccam, where we lodged that night, and on the 26th of the same month, having embarked in champans [a type of boat], we arrived again in Coaijonan in the forenoon with this fortunate victory (for which thanks must be given to the Almighty). text_translated_detailed: of the lands to the Netherlands state again received in grace, they marched on the twenty-second of December with aforementioned approximately five hundred white-clad, mostly well-trained soldiers, and about four to five hundred inhabitants from the villages of Sinckan, Soulangh, and Baccaluan toward the village of Pagcareijang, where Formosa Saccareijangh was taken and entirely burned with fire. After we had marched for a long time (having passed many beautiful flat fields, small woods, and small streams, as well as some large rivers), on the twenty-fifth of the same month around midday we arrived, and encountered some troops of theirs, who at first came very fiercely upon our Sinckan people and forward troops, but seeing some of theirs fall underfoot and be wounded, they began to retreat into the long reeds and some fled toward the village. Whereupon their pursuers followed and we took the village, which that same evening we set on fire, to prevent the escape or withdrawal of the inhabitants and to prevent them from following us. We made our camp in the flat field, where there was an abundance of long reeds and grass. According to the account that the Chinese and the Taccareijanders themselves gave us afterward, thirteen of theirs remained dead and six or so were wounded, although our inhabitants had obtained no more than nine heads, after which this nation is extremely eager. Of ours, none remained, and only two or three soldiers were wounded in the feet with foot-traps. The next day, being the twenty-sixth of the same month, we marched again toward Saccam, passing through a village that was situated about a quarter hour's journey from an extraordinarily large or broad but shallow river. We found everything burned, without a single house remaining standing, and as a certain sign that the inhabitants of the aforementioned village had surprised and murdered one of our Joncoken [small vessels] lying in the Jouckan River at night,

text_translated_detailed: wounded in the feet with foot-traps. The next day, being the twenty-sixth of the same month, we marched again toward Saccam, passing through a village that was situated about a quarter hour's journey from an extraordinarily large or broad but shallow river. We found everything burned, without a single house remaining standing, and as a certain sign that the inhabitants of the aforementioned village had surprised and murdered one of our Joncoken lying in the Jouckan River at night, we found the barrel of a Dutch musket and several pieces of clothing belonging to ours. Thus, by good fortune, the correct village that most deserved punishment was struck, which could easily have happened otherwise, since several villages were situated nearby, and we ourselves and our allied inhabitants did not know the truly guilty ones. The aforementioned river, which at that time had become a considerable stretch of dry land, showed itself on both sides and close behind us with large troops, who sought to pursue and encircle us if they could. Wherefore, with a certain troop of soldiers and almost all the inhabitants, we made a sharp counterattack upon them, which seeing that we were coming at them and that with the horses they could run so swiftly, they all immediately took to flight without pursuing us further. And thus we came—with this surpassing victory, which was esteemed extremely highly by the surrounding villages—thank God with a strong and healthy force by a shorter route on the twenty-eighth of the same month again to Saccam. This having thus fortunately occurred and been accomplished, they prepared the matter through a certain Soulanger, in order to bring into our hands most of all the guilty ones of the aforementioned village who had been occupied with the murder of a certain sick-comforter [chaplain], as well as those who had helped carry out the enormous deed with those of Mattauw, in the most convenient manner, and thus to protect the innocent from harm.

In order to bring this about, on the eighth of January in the year 1636, we marched over Sinckan with our previous force and a good party of Sinckan people in that direction, and arrived without any resistance or opposition a little before sunset in the aforementioned village, where at first most everything had fled, yet no one who appeared was given any offense or molestation. We made it known that we had come to make peace. Fifty-seven villages on Formosa lying are with the Netherlands state reconciled. The Pimabaers is a nation dwelling close by the gold mine, standing firm in weapons and Pangsoia, whether they were called or some enemies wished to wage war in the field to appear, or in the event of the stranding of any of our ships (which God forbid) with our flag to appear among ours, and thus to show all help and assistance. But principally to make it known to them that our friends are, and to prevent all the evils that might result from this. This having been done, each returned with joy to his village and we departed to Fort Zeelandia. This peace alone was maintained until our departure from Taijouan, which was on the fifteenth of November last past, firmly and very steadfastly with good contentment of each one, and was continued, but gradually now and then (as Your Excellency may be pleased to observe through a certain missive from Dominie Robertus Sumius addressed to Your Excellency) several other villages

This peace alone was maintained until our departure from Taijouan, which was on the fifteenth of November last past, firmly and very steadfastly with good contentment of each one, and was continued, but gradually now and then (as Your Excellency may be pleased to observe through a certain missive from Dominie Robertus Sumius addressed to Your Excellency) several other villages, some of which requested this of themselves and some resolved to do so upon our written request, were also brought under the general bond of peace, so that the number increased from twenty-two to fifty-seven villages, which the General Company has accepted and recognized as their protected lords, among which are certainly the most considerable, fifteen villages situated at the southern end of Formosa, whose inhabitants are called Lonckjouwers [Siraya people], who possess the land there to a good extent on the east and also west side and wage war against a certain nation called the Pimabaers, who according to the account of these Lonckjouwers are also seated on the east side of the mountains a considerable stretch to the north of them and wage war against the inhabitants who possess the gold mine. These aforementioned Ponckjauwers are much better civilized than the inhabitants of some of the aforementioned villages. The women as well as the men all go clothed, and are governed by a chief (whom they greatly respect) as by a sovereign prince, who enjoys his share or portion of everything that is sown or reaped, as well as from the hunt, and in place of tribute he takes from them. The brother of this aforementioned chief came as a hostage of ours in Taijouan to negotiate peace with us. In the meantime, there also appeared those of Lonckjau in Taijouan, the chief of Pangsoia, who also has the supreme authority there over some of his villages,

text_translated_detailed: The Chinese trade has grown considerably from time to time, and in the year 1636 it has been remarkably improved. The costly ship Zutphen, having lost two anchors and ropes, after its rudder had been driven onto the rocks, was driven with its side into a small bay against the shore without the hull touching bottom, where it remained lying until the next day, when with the help of the yacht Waterloose Werve another anchor was brought to sea and (being still tight) was cut off from it. The proof of whether the same goods are genuine and unadulterated can be taken as follows: whenever one pours a little into a clean porcelain cup and stirs and rubs the same with a linen or woolen cloth on the bottom, then if the same is not good, some small grains will remain stuck to the cloth, and if it is good, little or nothing at all will stick to it. text_translated_detailed: Among our Dutch nation are called satins, but since we have already made mention of common satins at length, we shall here speak only of plain as well as figured, all manner of colored and black as well as white satins. The good or best black, all manner of colored as well as white plain satins are made from extraordinarily fine silk in Canton and thereabouts, the black weighing from 35 to 37 taels [modern equivalent: approximately 1.3-1.4 kg] according to whether they are fine or coarse in silk and are ordinarily about 30 ells [modern equivalent: approximately 18 meters] long, likewise the colored as well as white 30 to 34 taels heavy and long as before. These are commonly purchased here—the colored and white which have appeared here only sparingly thus far—at 8 to 9 reals [modern equivalent: Spanish colonial currency], and the black according to how fine they are, 8, 9, and also well 10 reals per piece. One should not pay too much attention to the weight unless they are very fine in luster and fine in silk and well struck in the weaving, since if the fineness or luster is lacking therein, the weight is then a bad sign that the silk has been damaged in the dyeing, whereby such satins then commonly become worn in wearing and are inclined to tear. For some time now we have received a fairly large quantity of such black satins which, although made in Canton and previously seemed fine, were greatly damaged in the dyeing of the silk, were loosely struck in the weaving, were calendered [modern equivalent: pressed and smoothed] too much, and moreover the greater part of the back half was entirely poor and nearly unusable, such that we were forced to—as this was brought to Canton—open these satins and the coarse-grained silk mostly entirely and completely unroll them to find the damage, and the Chinese, on account of the great trouble that is attached to this, have taken an aversion to sending such defective goods here anymore, under protest that if they were to continue therein we would be forced to burn everything.

text_translated_detailed: Linen, powder, sugar, sugar chests, black sugar, blue [dye], and likewise the raw [materials] (although some have been drawn for the provision of clothing, yet the same can always be obtained if the merchants are warned two to three months in advance). Of the finest sort, in the previous monsoon we also obtained some sea-green [cloth] to be used for clothing the common folk, as well as some other colors that were dyed and sent to Batavia [Jakarta], but we receive no answer as to whether they were well received there, which we trust they were, yes, since they stand quite beautifully and inexpensively compared to other fabrics for clothing the soldiers. When some are brought, one can use the same here among the common folk, as well as in Batavia at three-eighths to one rixdaler [modern equivalent: Dutch silver coin] per piece (provided they are properly fine). Well, regarding two to three thousand pieces of old and silver linen, they are of such varied length, width, and quality that the same cannot well be written down in order, but best by the sample thereof being with the Company shall be purchased. Regarding this, our further bearing: oyster sugar amounts to two million pounds. As much as can be obtained for the homeland and three to forty pounds for Persia is requested. With the same, in the previous year, one-quarter to one-quarter rixdaler per picul [modern equivalent: unit of weight, approximately 60 kg] in price was to be increased. It has flowed to us so abundantly that this monsoon, as you are aware, there were scarcely ships enough to carry the sugar over, more than the demand could satisfy. Wherefore now henceforth (unless through a poor harvest) it shall not need to be increased in price anymore. The quality consists in the dry whiteness, as well as the coarseness and glitter of the grain. Item, that the same is not forty fat, eighteen meal, and gray, upon which close regard must be taken. Ditto is worth two and one-half when gray. Two and three-quarters, two and two-thirds, three rixdaler, and three and one-half to three and one-quarter rixdaler when wholly white.

text_translated_detailed: The Chinese trade is praiseworthy, but when opinions and personal interests run counter to this, they have proven themselves harmful. Important places must be served with good care and carefully guarded. To clarify in what manner and way the rich and excellent Chinese or Taiwanese trade shall be preserved against certain approaching difficulties, and the Company's position and circumstances on the island of Formosa [Taiwan] be better secured, we present this to the Honorable Governor General Antonio van Diemen [Antonio van Diemen] and the Esteemed Honorable Council of India, explaining this in the most concise and brief manner possible. text_translated_detailed: We might thus, by the grace of the Emperor, make known that once the purpose, which is a free and unencumbered trade, is achieved, and the Portuguese thereby struggle out of it—which God willing, as it may succeed to the good of the Honored Company, Amen. Furthermore, it is necessary, as for the Kings of Persia, Carnatic, Pegu, Arakan, Mataram, Achin, and other rulers of India, to send (with the first opportunity, as was requested in the year 1637) the following 20 pieces of fine cloth of the following colors: 4 pieces crimson red, 4 pieces green, 4 pieces purple, 2 pieces black, 2 pieces green, 2 pieces ash-gray, 2 pieces violet. 20 pieces of satin of the same colors except black. 6 to 8 pieces of the richest and heaviest gold cloth, mostly red and green, and no blue. 5 to 6 pieces of paintings of battle scenes, naval engagements, and the like, with their frames—the larger the more pleasing. 6 large round or globe mirrors, to be used as gifts. 12 pieces of triangular, cut glass giving off various colors. And besides the common mirrors called speculation glass, 4 pieces of gold buckles, each of particular and handsome enameled design. 30 dozens of fine English and other made knives, of which half with silver handles. 6 pieces of large, fine elk hides, and 20 good pieces of calf hides, of which five with gold passementerie borders—these have been requested for two years for various princes, but until now nothing has been received to the Company's detriment. And by continuation, a supply of paints, brushes, and small brushes for counterfeiting for His Majesty in Persia. 10 pieces of very fine cambric cloth. 25 pieces of gold galloon. 15 pieces of gold passementerie of 3 to 4 types. For Batavia and the surrounding quarters of India: 60 pieces of sempiternal cloth of various colors for clothing for the garrison as well as in Batavia, Moluccas, Amboina, Banda, and Taiwan. 4,500 pairs of shoes.

Also some good fine sealing thread. And let it be remembered that in the packing of the cases which are sent hereward, no shoes should be packed with hats, nor should hats be packed with anything else, for the one, by reason of the moisture, and the other by reason of the greasiness, both hats and shoes, spoil in various packages, whether of cloth, perpetuanas [a type of fabric], hats, and the like. Gray paper with spikes and fly-smeared, conserved in this manner for prevention, extraordinarily well. Upon which Your Excellency would be pleased to provide the necessary equipment for the naval forces coming hereward, which we request of Your Excellency be fulfilled as promptly as possible. In particular, anchors, cables, sails, canvas, and the like. Of which this past year, by reason of the spillage on the coast of China and other quarters, has been extraordinarily scarce, indeed so much so that we have not been able to send supplies to various quarters without great concern and fear of some considerable disaster. Therefore, Your Excellency we kindly request that attention be paid and also consideration given that these requested necessities be sent to us with the first opportunity. 50 pieces of anchors of 10, 12, 13, 14, and 1500 pounds. 60 pieces of rope of 100 to 800 pounds. 60 pieces of dredges of 50 to 130 pounds.

text_translated_detailed: General Antonio van Diemen. To the esteemed and most worthy Governor and most earnest, wise, and provident very generous lord. According to the resolution made in our previous [document] herewith in copy, dated the 5th of August last, in the ship Wasse, toward the roadstead in the islands of Pehouw, on the following day with the aforementioned ship, together with the Gallias and Groll, set sail, and between the 27th and 28th, being there 22 days' journey, on account of the northerly winds and great calm before the strait of Coetchi, God be praised, we arrived well and with pleasure. We learned from the oral report of the chief merchant Larons as well as from the written notes or daily register kept during my absence that the Company's present constitution had no further determination in the matter of the silk trade that had occurred, but the supplicant's request from the five imperial cities (notwithstanding that the same was delivered with many attached false and untrue statements to the detriment of the Netherlands by the old regent Findad and the Imperial Council) was flatly rejected by the Council lord Sanincked on the 3rd of April last with some reproaching reasons. The former Governor Pieter Nuijts was released from his detention and permitted to depart with the first ships. The Company's ships, when they desired, by means of a passing written act to the regents of Nagasaki, were not to call upon any galleons sailing from Japan and were freely permitted to depart. Nor did they need to request permission from those of Nagasaki to unload or discharge the first arriving ships or ship, but this was done by those of Firando, just as with Groll, together with Wassenaer, on the same day of our arrival within Firando. Here comes also the mild gift of 200 schuit [units] of silver which His Imperial Majesty gave to the Dutch commissioners, which, as a token of honor, rings throughout all Japan, whereas such a donation was never before given to the Portuguese and Dutch or other foreign nations unless they were vassals.

We learned from the oral report of the chief merchant Larons as well as from the written notes or daily register kept during my absence that the Company's present constitution had no further determination in the matter of the silk trade that had occurred, but the supplicant's request from the five imperial cities (notwithstanding that the same was delivered with many attached false and untrue statements to the detriment of the Netherlands by the old regent Findad and the Imperial Council) was flatly rejected by the Council lord Sanincked on the 3rd of April last with some reproaching reasons. The former Governor Pieter Nuijts was released from his detention and permitted to depart with the first ships. The Company's ships, when they desired, by means of a passing written act to the regents of Nagasaki, were not to call upon any galleons sailing from Japan and were freely permitted to depart. Nor did they need to request permission from those of Nagasaki to unload or discharge the first arriving ships or ship, but this was done by those of Firando, just as with Groll, together with Wassenaer, on the same day of our arrival within Firando. Here comes also the mild gift of 200 schuit units of silver which His Imperial Majesty gave to the Dutch commissioners, which, as a token of honor, rings throughout all Japan, whereas such a donation was never before given to the Portuguese and Dutch or other foreign nations unless they were vassals.

text_translated_detailed: happened and on the 7th of March arrived in Meaco [Kyoto], we understood from one of the Gentlemen of the Lord of Firando [Hirado] the great desire of His Excellency and the Council Lord Tackimon [uncertain: possibly Takimon] regarding the Dutch commission. However, with the answer over this matter and the order raised previously here, he seemed entirely content. Among other reasons, His Excellency related the discontent of the Governor of Nagasaki against the Dutch nation, which consisted in our bold arrogance, fearing no one, the living and trading in such a way that we neither respect the Majesty and his commands nor the persons who governed in his name, did what came into our minds, and thereby boasted that our principals had commanded us thus, as if wishing thereby to show that we would live in Japan according to the order of our masters as well as the customs of our quarters, etc. By the requests or petitions of the five imperial cities (in order to obtain the Dutch as well as the Portuguese and Chinese white raw silk under lock and key and to be distributed among the subordinates and chief officials of the said cities qualified for that purpose) these unheard-of and false accusations were added and delivered to the Council Lord Saninckedo [uncertain: possibly Sanin Kedo]. However, according to the Council Lord Jackimondo [uncertain: possibly Takimondo] and His Excellency's custom as well as other of our friends, the petitioners stood to obtain nothing in their made requests but were flatly rejected. For which reason the matter concerning ours could not rest easy, and the fear of the same falling upon the Company's neck was thrown upon us.

It was true that the Chinese junks had previously been mastered and the goods priced, the great ones of the aforementioned realm had not kept their solemn promises of trade and free commerce. text_translated_detailed: Copy of Resolutions on the Voyage from Batavia to the Fatherland by the Honorable Governor Hansputmans and the council of the ships Banda and New Zealand. Drawn up on Tuesday, being the thirtieth of December in the year 1636, in the ship Banda lying a little north of the Long Island at anchor. The Broad Council of the ships Banda, New Zealand, Zutphen, Prinswillem, and Leeuwarden, gathered and called together by the Honorable Putmans, gives, after having read a certain conceived letter, the same into consideration, whether or not any of his seals or signs for further instruction, with better and more thorough knowledge and prevention of all abuses, by force or otherwise should be dealt with, or whether the same already conceived in such form should be maintained and observed throughout the entire fleet, and thereafter followed. A second matter: what ration of meat and bacon above oil, vinegar, and bread one should distribute weekly, likewise rice, arrack, and water daily throughout the entire fleet among the people. And third: whether one should also allow some under-officers, assistants, and surgeons, as has been the custom on some ships sailing in the land, also to eat in the cabin, or whether the same should be placed on such rations as the order with the ships from the fatherland comes from our Honorable Lords and Masters. On all which points, after having made an examination of the victuals over the respective fleet for the completion of the voyage, serious consideration being given, it is, for various good insights and motives, by a vote found good to do the following, namely: First, the said letter in such form as the same has been established by his Excellency, so distributed throughout the entire fleet, and on each article, as is proper, shall be read and observed, on pain of that being touched upon, whoever remains in default or fails. Second, first throughout the entire fleet

text_translated_detailed: Given as above. Undersigned: Hans Putmans, A. Anthonissen, Thijs Quast, Davit de Solemne, Denijs Anthonisz, V. Dries, E. Ebbegine. Saturday the 3rd of January, Year 1637. Considering that during the preceding night we came to approximately ½ mile [approximately 0.8 kilometers] west of the island across in the way, we encountered such a vehement current that not only did we lose our daily and duty anchor with two new ropes, and 2 miles [approximately 3.2 kilometers] east of the island were driven into a very helpless strait, but also three of our ships, namely Sutphen, Prince Willem, and Leeuwarden, were separated and the same were driven out of sight, and moreover upon our departure from Batavia we also left behind an anchor and rope that broke there while being hauled up, such that no more than three anchors and three good ropes remain with the ship Banda present, remaining. Likewise the costly ship Sutphen with its side against the shore on the same small island found lying motionless, which with the help of their small boats and the aforesaid ship's boat with an anchor at sea, was brought again to 25 fathoms [approximately 45.7 meters] of water in the float, though not in such a safe road as was well required for the security of so costly a ship. Wherefore, in order for the Honored Lord Gijssels and Putmans to bring the speediest pre-warning of this sorrowful misfortune and yet to secure the same ship as much as possible, they had taken counsel with the other to leave the aforesaid yacht's small boat there in order to bring out two more anchors and to dispatch the same yacht to Bantam or where the aforesaid Lords might find it necessary. In which sailing from the aforesaid Pigs' Point strait-ward in approximately one mile or another half of that from there under the mentioned coast of Sumatra, we found lying at anchor the ship Leeuwarden, which had also lost two anchors and ropes and had been in the utmost danger of running against the cliffs. Because we, from the report of the Honorable Governor Hansputmans arriving here yesterday evening, have understood the sorrowful and lamentable misfortune that befell the Honorable Company in the loss of their Return ship Prince Willem on the coast of Sumatra, near the Pigs' Point, it has been, at the request of the aforementioned Honorable Governor Hans Puttmans, who proposed that not only the return ships in general, through the great tempests that they have endured, were completely and entirely stripped of anchors and ropes, and therefore needed to be provided at the very least with ten anchors and ten cables again. Item, that the ship Zutphen, in the utmost danger, having lost its course, was still lying at anchor within the Cliffs near the aforementioned point, expecting assistance. However, according to the report of the overseer of the water-works, nothing other than that the aforementioned ship, at flood tide on the 22nd or 23rd of [uncertain: vaemwaeters] [modern equivalent: fathoms], ground, brought approximately half a cable's length from the shore, where assistance was being awaited. Moreover, it was put forward that the commanders of the ships Wassenaer and the galley have been ordered to salvage the cargo of the wrecked ship from before and near Bantam, and it would be useful to order some other ships as well for their assistance. For these reasons, it has been deemed necessary in all respects to proceed with the greatest speed and to provide the aforementioned return ships anew with ten anchors according to the requirement put forward by the Honorable Mister Governor Puttmans.

On Thursday, the Assembled Council, upon the proposition and request of Mister Sebalt Wouderaer and provisional receiver on behalf of the General Dutch East India Company in Batavia, the which he brought forward and related how that he, before his departure from there, had been charged and commissioned by the Honorable Gentlemen, the Governor-General and Council of India, after having conducted a muster of the return ships here lying ready and destined for the Fatherland, to transport himself with the ship the galley to Bantam's anchorage and to report to the King, while their Honors had since some time been instructed and notified by express order of the King on several occasions that His Majesty was entirely and completely inclined toward a new peace with the General Company, provided that such Javanese prisoners, 31 in number, as we had captured from them during this war and had held captive in Batavia until now, were sent to him and restored to him, on the condition that he would likewise allow the Company's Dutch prisoners to come to us, and that he would, in the name and on behalf of the aforementioned Honorable Gentlemen, the Governor-General and Council of India, likewise declare, affirm, and make known to the same King their Honors' good and sincere inclination toward peace, and that their Honors, to satisfy the King's demand and desire for the restitution of the aforementioned 31 Javanese, had sent them to be restored to His Majesty, and thereby to demonstrate and make clear to all the world that peace is sincerely meant by their Honors.

text_translated_detailed: Piettersz Uithoeck. Wednesday the 28th of January in the year 1637. In the ship Banda lying at anchor under Sebesse. Observed on today, yesterday, and the day before yesterday, sometimes one and sometimes two, whether English or of our ships have been across in the sea, and the westerly winds are still blowing so hard that the English ship London, having departed from here yesterday to pursue its journey to Cape of Good Hope, has come back here through storm to us at the anchorage, and the captain of the aforementioned ship is presenting us his boat to exchange at the coast of Sumatra some provisions such as fruit trees for our refreshment — provided that the yacht Waterloose Werve also goes there to bring the provisions and otherwise back here, yes even if they are in need of money to advance us so much cash, His Excellency Governor Putmans gives the council in all seriousness to consider whether one should accept this presentation given that there are already many sick in the two ships — and daily through the continuous rain many more are falling ill, or whether for some considerations — one should neglect this. Upon which with careful deliberation it was unanimously with his Excellency deemed good to let the yacht Waterloose Werve sail to the high land of Sumatra together with the English boat to obtain, as mentioned above, refreshment for our sick, to refresh the same somewhat, and in the meantime our ships shall wait until the 30th of this month. Going with the ship Banda toward Texel the ships Amsterdam, the Hope, Zeelandia, Saint Pietter, and the trow yacht, and with the ship New Zealand the ships Zeeusche Leeuw [Zeeland Lion], Arnemuiden, the Hen, and Waxing Moon. Item, the trow yacht shall enter Texel in order to obtain there according to the order of the Lords commissioned directors, and in case finding no one there to go out again, during which time the other ships shall remain set ahead, and if within the time of 24 hours no advice is received, they shall then at the speediest pursue their journey again according to their order toward Feril. In like manner, the ships that go toward Zeeland shall on the first [opportunity] with advice from land (be it with one or another vessel) anchor for the time of 24 hours ahead, and receiving no advice—as before, pursue their journeys without waiting for the ships from Texel, nor also those from Texel to theirs, but each at the speediest set their journey toward Feril—To wit (when it is deemed advisable to separate from one another) shall by the ships Banda and Zeelandia a pennant of the great mast—wave, and if the others find this advisable shall do likewise, as when each shall join himself to his ordered ship. Dated as above. Understood. Hans Putmans, Jan Attesz, Adriaen Anthonissen, Thijs Quast, this is the mark of Lievensz, Cornelis Davit de Solemne, Denijs Anthonisz van Drien, Frans Leendertsz Valck

text_translated_detailed: Copy of the Daily Register Kept on the Ship Banda of the Voyage from Batavia to the Fatherland, Beginning on the 29th of December 1636 and Ending on the 29th of December. In the evening, the Esteemed Governor Putmans departs as Commander over this year destined for the return voyage to the Fatherland. Return ships, namely Banda, Nieuw Zeelandt [New Zealand], Zutphen, Prins Willem [Prince William], and Leeuwarden, to begin his journey there, whereupon the following day the ship Nieuwenck Huijsen is to follow, and at the Cape of Good Hope the ships Swol and Amelia are still to join. May God Almighty guide us with the aforementioned ships for a speedy and safe arrival at our desired destination. Around 3 o'clock in the evening, because of the sharp wind, we came alongside the Long Island at 13 fathoms [approximately 78 feet] of sticking ground and anchored. The mentioned island lies approximately a quarter mile south-southeast of us. On the 30th, the wind shifted to the land, and with the entire fleet we weighed anchor and set our course west and west-by-east toward Point Babij, except for the ship Leeuwarden, which had positioned itself too close under the anchorage and had to make one or two casts before it could get under sail. For a short time during the day it was calm, and it was decided by the Broad Council of the Fleet that the sailing letter be drawn up by the Esteemed Governor Putmans and read aloud in council and approved. Likewise, regarding the provisioning of the crew, so that everything among the entire fleet could be done in good order and equally, without confusion, each captain was given a provisioning letter containing the following, namely: For the week ahead, thirteen days of meat and bacon, namely three-quarters and one-half pound noted over the meat and bacon for every man of the entire fleet. Four bean days, one-half pound for each man per day, namely Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday night. One mug of olive oil and one measure of vinegar for each person.

text_translated_detailed: Confusion could be avoided, and each captain was given a provisioning letter containing the following, namely: For the week ahead, thirteen days of meat and bacon, namely three-quarters and one-half pound noted over the meat and bacon for every man of the entire fleet. Four bean days, one-half pound for each man per day, namely Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday night. One mug of olive oil and one measure of vinegar for each person. Five pounds of bread for each person. Three measures of rice for each man, for each meal, for all these days throughout the entire fleet, to be provisioned as much as possible. One and one-half mugs of arrack [a type of distilled spirit] for each man. Eight mugs of water for each person. On this date it was also deemed good, to prevent all confusion and dispute among the common folk, and to follow our Lords and Masters' orders as much as possible, that all under-steersmen, assistants, and surgeons, outside of the cabin, shall eat and be provisioned for the same as ordered, likewise also for the bricklayers. Toward evening, due to contrary wind, we were one mile west of the Cannibal Island at 6 fathoms of water, being sticking ground. On the 31st of the same month, two hours before daybreak, we weighed anchor in the land wind and went under sail, our course west and west-by-north. During the day it was again calm, and after midday we had favorable wind weather. On the same day, a Master Evij, a merchant of the English Company, came with some letters from the president to be delivered to the English Company at London, which the Esteemed Governor Putmans accepted and took upon himself to deliver. In the evening, the first watch being over, we anchored under the west point of Bantam at 16 fathoms of sticking ground. On the 1st of January in the year 1636, in the morning the wind was westerly but variable.

text_translated_detailed: And after midday we had favorable wind weather. On the same day, a Master Evij, a merchant of the English Company, came with some letters from the president to be delivered to the English Company at London, which the Esteemed Governor Putmans accepted and took upon himself to deliver. In the evening, the first watch being over, we anchored under the west point of Bantam at 16 fathoms of sticking ground. On the 1st of January in the year 1636, in the morning the wind was westerly but variable, and we found the current running out of the strait. We weighed anchor and went under sail. Toward midday we received a southerly wind and let it carry us westward toward the coast of Sumatra. In the first watch it became calm, and we anchored at 30 to 35 fathoms under one of the small islands lying close under the coast of Sumatra, across from Varken's Point [Pig's Point]. On the 2nd of the same month, in the morning the wind was west-southwest. We weighed anchor and made our way between the mentioned Varken's Point and across the passage to get through. On the same day, after the inspection and muster of the ships had been completed, 145 men were counted on the entire fleet. Among them many were found to be unfit, whereupon it was deemed good by Mr. Gijssels and Putmans with the commissioned council members (considering that the ships nevertheless remained adequately manned) that the Banda, in place of 110, be manned with 110; Nieuw Zeelandt, in place of 110, with 146; Zutphen, in place of 110, with 123; Prins Willem, in place of 110, with 95; and Leeuwarden, in place of 100, with 117 men. And no more than 23 were to be steered back to Batavia, the more so since their time was already completely up. And so Mr. Gijssels with the commissioned men on the ships Wassenaar and the galiot of Hoorn, a little before midday (after they had taken their leave of Governor Putmans and other departing friends) went to Bantam to meet the peace there.

text_translated_detailed: Zutphen, in place of 110, with 123; Prins Willem, in place of 110, with 95; and Leeuwarden, in place of 100, with 117 men. And no more than 23 were to be steered back to Batavia, the more so since their time was already completely up. And so Mr. Gijssels with the commissioned men on the ships Wassenaar and the galiot of Hoorn, a little before midday (after they had taken their leave of Governor Putmans and other departing friends) went to Bantam to meet the peace there, departing in January of the year 1636. We left the yacht Waterloose to convoy us outside the strait. During our stay, around midday, when the breeze began to diminish and we were crossing the passage, we still sailed southwest toward the coast of Java until about three hours after midday, when the coast of Java had drawn near and the ships Nieuw Zeelandt, Zutphen, and Leeuwarden were still under the coast of Sumatra. The weather with Prins Willem turned toward Sumatra. Toward evening we came back again (across from Varken's Point) to our aforementioned other ships, but since it was not high enough above the mentioned point to obtain good anchorage, we could not sail. We turned the entire fleet southward again and received at times a somewhat stiffer breeze, with small squalls, such that our fore-topsail sheet came to break and tore across the entire yard. However, we quickly got the sheet clear again, and the ship was repaired, each one doing his best to recover somewhat and to obtain good anchorage. Around 2 or 3 hours in the evening we received squall upon squall with hard wind and rain, such that we could scarcely take in our sails in 3 or 4 hours [a watch period], the same being true for all the other ships, which were very close to one another.

text_translated_detailed: Wassenaer is sailing forward toward Bantam, and Mr. Putmans with the yacht Water Loose Werve (running before the wind) is doing his best to still arrive at Batavia on the same day. About two hours before evening, he arrived there with the aforementioned yacht, and the sad news reached Mr. Philips Lucassen and the accompanying council. The Honorable General departed on the 30th of last month with seventeen sail toward Amboyna, as was reported by Mr. Putman, with the request that assistance be provided as quickly and as much as would be possible. On the 5th of the same month, in the morning, it was agreed upon by the Honorable Messrs. Philips Lucassen and Hans Putmans, together with the accompanying council members Goessens, de Widt, and van der Lijn, to provision the solace fleet with the following items: namely, ten anchors, five new ropes, and thirty to forty barrels of water, four barrels of arrack [a type of distilled spirit], eight good planks for a rudder for the Zutphen, likewise anchor stocks, and whatever else was necessary, along with some spars and diving equipment and other gear in order to salvage the unfortunate cargo as much as possible and to send it by way of the fluyt ship Schaegen, along with Water Loose Werve and Hooge Caspel, as quickly as possible with the equipment and Master Cornelis Schouten to that location, and that the Honorable Mr. Putmans shall depart again this very evening in order to resume his journey with the ships Banda, Nieuw Zeeland, Zutphen, and Leeuwarden as soon as it is possible toward the Cape of Good Hope, to which may Almighty God grant His merciful blessing. On the same day, there were very heavy labors on the roadstead, such that according to the statement of the Equipment Master, scarcely anything could be accomplished with such heavy work. A little in the evening, there came a hard northwest wind, followed by much rain.

The same, around three o'clock at midday, we tacked inside, inside Gaets and came, a little bit, God be praised, with strong and healthy people inside the Helder at anchor. During our voyage from Batavia [Jakarta] as well on the ship Zeelandia as Banda, we lost in total ten men, the governor among them, who mostly died in part through natural sickness, according to form.

text_translated_detailed: Instructions for the Commander Adrian [Adriaan] Anthonis and further council persons of the ships Groote Warmont and Huisduinen, according to which they shall conduct themselves upon sailing from here and further to Batavia [Jakarta], is as follows in the most necessary manner and very generous governor as the Lord [God] may [grant]. Since the dispatch of the fluyt ship De Swaan dated the 2nd [of the month], we have been able to give, with which the copy of our previous [dispatch] dated the 19th September and 23rd October have been sent to you, here on the 5th and 6th [of the month] from China have arrived well, five junks with a shipment of sugar and Cangas dye [a red dye], likewise on the 8th of the same month there came to the coast the long-awaited silk junk with approximately 250 picul [modern equivalent: ~136 metric tons] raw silk, 61 catties [modern equivalent: ~36 kg] of gold and a shipment of silk fabrics mostly for Japan and not for us in Pedro, it seemed to the patria [homeland] serviceable. Of which aforementioned silk no more than 150 picul of the same could be found serviceable for the fatherland, with which Your Excellency's requirement for the patria (concerning the silk) is satisfied. The remainder, Indian wax, was quite a bit coarser; otherwise Your Excellency would have had more shipment sent. To be placed [in the account], the same shall come wholly. The gold and the Cangas dye, being approximately 80 picul, in fluyts [small vessels] have been transferred. We have all together, besides a good shipment of pearls and large fine porcelain dishes (which with the Swaan they had intended to throw overboard, and now as ballast of the yacht Venloo with 20 [uncertain: measurement or quantity] red Chinese [goods] with itself one here alongside go) and further as much sugar as the General's yacht has been able to load, have been shipped therein, as Your Excellency from the invoice and the bill of lading will be pleased to observe. May God Almighty let the same arrive with good fortune at the proper and timely cost in safety. Regarding the purchase of the same silk, we understood that his fellow trader with approximately 100 picul silk and a shipment of fabrics loaded, being likewise still another with a shipment of sugar and silk, were soon to follow. Likewise, that they from various persons with a Chinese junk over Quelang in Japan in Hoecheo [uncertain: place name] had arrived, understood that the pancado [a tax or duty system] in Japan by his Imperial Majesty had been entirely abolished. The silk [sold for] 360 [currency], the red silks 5 to 6, the velvets which were good 10 and 12, the white sugar 10, and the black 11 to 12 taels [modern equivalent: ~37-44 grams per tael]. Had good [sales]. Then likewise it appears that this monsoon no Portuguese vessels arrived in Japan, but two Dutch ships lay before Nagasaki and the rest without being able to name the number under Firando at the roadstead. What shall come of this pleasant news, time will tell. The General's merchants reported likewise that a certain great English ship had arrived before Macao, and there negotiated with the Portuguese (having also brought a great capital), and also the silk rose well 4 to 5 taels per picul there, through which in China [prices] had risen. What shall come of this, we doubt not, or Your Excellency shall know the truth better and sooner than we can learn here.

text_translated_detailed:
Instruction for the Esteemed Commandeur Adriaen Anthonis and further council members of the ships Groene, Warmont, and Huijsduijnen, according to which they shall conduct themselves upon sailing from here to Quinam [Quanzhou/Fujian] and thereafter to Batavia.

The Esteemed Commandeur and further council members are hereby made aware, according to the most recent resolution dated the 5th current, how necessary this voyage to Quinam is, at the utmost speed (so that the Esteemed Governors General may yet have timely advice regarding the Quinam trade and the success in proceeding with the 23,580 rixdollars [modern equivalent: silver coins] of eight reals, which by his majesty's authority are to be recovered from the wrecked ship Grooten, which is to be obtained). Accordingly, you are all most seriously recommended to undertake your journey as soon as you have departed from here in God's name, sailing south of the island Pekuw [uncertain: possibly Penghu/Pescadores] directly toward the coast of China, in order to avoid five or six miles to the north or windward of Pedro Branca [uncertain: possibly a coastal landmark], and to bring the same into sight, so that you may thereby set a nearer and more certain course outside the islands of Machauw [Macau], Poulo Taijo [uncertain: possibly Taipa], and the like, directly toward the small islands of Tinhosa [uncertain: possibly Lema Islands], situated close to the great island Amoan [Amoy/Xiamen], continuing thereafter along the coast of Amoan until the same begins to stretch wholly toward the west, at which point you shall leave it and sail toward the island Campelo [uncertain: possibly Quemoy/Kinmen], and on the south or southwest side proceed to the proper anchorage, close under the shore to drop anchor.

Should you find any Spaniards or Portuguese anchored under the aforementioned islands, you shall endeavor to bring them into your power with the least bloodshed, provided that you prevent their escape as much as possible. In the event that (their capital being of little value) his majesty of Quinam should demand the restitution most urgently, such that the same might exercise trade there and the Company's payment might be secured, the means held back would be able to effect the restitution in proper form. However, it shall first be necessary to investigate whether his majesty is willing to pay a reasonable compensation for what has been recovered. And although his majesty's heart may remain set upon the restitution of our enemy's means, we nevertheless understand that in the event that upon making an assessment it should be discovered that the prince owes more than our claim against his majesty of Quinam amounts to, then in such a case the restitution shall not be understood to be demanded, even if we should have to return fruitlessly to Batavia. But rather, as has been said before, to throw him a good bone in his mouth, such that he shall refuse until further order from the Esteemed Governor General, provided that the King of Quinam is then made to understand what awaits him on account of his improper conduct in the seizure of our means. As soon as you have anchored under the aforementioned island, the chief merchant Abram Duijcker, together with another person from the council, with his majesty's Caesar or someone else, and furthermore three or four soldiers, using the least display according to Japanese customs (which here in Quinam appear still to be observed), shall proceed to Phipho [uncertain: possibly a place name] and from there to the old King, together with the Esteemed Governor General's letter and our accompanying missive, as well as the customary gifts in the best manner possible, which shall be transported with the utmost speed, and request an audience to speak with his majesty in person. Having obtained this, the aforementioned Duijcker, after having paid his respects, shall make it understood to his majesty that he is expressly commissioned by the Esteemed Governor General to obtain the restitution of the 23,580 rixdollars of eight reals, as silver coins, which our people brought in the boat of the wrecked yacht Grooten in the year 1634, expecting to find our ships on his majesty's roadstead, and which were seized against all right and justice by his majesty's subjects and delivered to his majesty, together with the goods of the wrecked yacht the Kemphaen. From his majesty, in all justice, to request the restitution, not doubting (in view of his majesty's reliance upon the account of the anachoda Kijko regarding the sugar account, or not) that in all rightful manner the restitution of the said monies, whether in gold or in cash, together with the cannon and further goods of the yacht the Kemphaen, to avoid all unpleasantness, shall be graciously rendered at present. This shall be done with such discretion and fundamental reasoning as the matter requires and the circumstances will permit, further referring to the Esteemed Governor General's authority, as in our missive.

text_translated_detailed: The Yacht Veenhuijs, which on the 2nd of the current month was to go from here to Wancan with stone and a party of timber works, on the 3rd in the evening departed from there and was caught that night by hard wind and until the 3rd has not been encountered by anyone in the Viscadores or hereabouts, but according to all appearances has been driven away, it is likely not, or shall be found by you in Quinam, as the said skipper heard in our discourse that the Yacht was intended to be used for the trade of Quinam, himself requested to exchange against the skipper of Schagen, making the guess that the same, being about to depart for Batavia, and moreover without doubt will have gone to Quinam. The said Yacht, if found there, shall, if the service of the general Company requires it this monsoon, be retained until the arrival and further order from Batavia, but no other ships that are laden with returns for Batavia. In place of the Witjes [type of goods] or senes in the mentioned ships, sugar shall be loaded, as much white sugar as can be obtained there, and the said ships can carry to the lowest price obtainable on purchase and to Batavia to be cleared, in case of lack of white price black, if the same can be obtained at a civil price of one to one and a half rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] per picul [modern equivalent: unit of weight, approximately 60 kg]. As soon as His Majesty of Quinam has made this restitution of the Company's means in whole or in part, and has granted the freedom to exercise trade there to Mr. Duycker at court, the said Duycker shall with the greatest speed inform the Commander and the council thereof, and at the same time, if he himself does not come without delay from Jan [uncertain: possibly a place name]), shall send word at once, as the said Duycker first deems necessary for the advancement of trade, so that everything without losing time may proceed with the greatest speed and the ships Grol, Warmont, and Huijsduijnen, still around the 8th to 10th of March may begin their journey to Batavia. If any Chinese junks are found at anchor in Quinam, you shall leave them unharmed and any encountered at sea shall be allowed to pass and repass freely, likewise all Cham merchants, Cambodians, and Quinammers, but all Chinese junks that you, departing from Quinam, might encounter near Poulo Timaon, Pansjam, or the east point of Linga, and tending toward Patani, Pahsan, Jambi, Andregi Rij, or the Strait of Malacca, you shall secure with people (without however harming the people in any way) and also bring to Batavia, governing ourselves further in this matter according to the instruction of the Esteemed Governor General given to the Commander also on the return voyage. And noting that we from the fluyt-ship Schagen on the 8th and 10th of January departed from the bay Manckan to Pehuw to fetch stone and the Yacht Veenhuijs with stone, timber works, and other necessities on the first of this month departed from here to the aforesaid bay Wanckan, until now has not appeared there nor has anything been heard of anywhere, so that according to all appearances it has been driven away, and for reasons mentioned before we shall expect it in Quinam, so the Esteemed Commander and the council are most seriously recommended, if the same is found there, to take careful regard as to what kind of ship upon obtaining trade there shall best be retained, whether Schagen in place of Veenhuijs or whether, considering that Schagen is the most suitable ship to return to Batavia with the first required merchandise from Batavia), Warmont's lading shall be transferred to Schagen and Veenhuijs, Warmont with the senes shall remain there, provided that Schagen and Veenhuijs shall then be cleared to Batavia, to which we trust, as Schagen draws very shallow water and can be loaded here first and come in, the Company shall be served best, the more so as Warmont is quite large to load the black sugar for Japan, for which otherwise an empty ship from Batavia would have to be sent there. The Company's affairs being handled in the best manner possible in Quinam in this way, the Commander with the aforementioned ships shall make his journey with the greatest speed, directing his course from the Island Campelo outside the island Poelo Caton Laur and in sight of the coast of Champa to the island Poulo Cicier de Terre, from where straight through the sea between the islands Anambas and Poulo Timaon, straight to the South point of Linga without touching any islands unless the greatest necessity requires it) shall cross over to better hasten his journey, continuing from the said South point to the East point of Linga straight toward and through the strait Palumban de Simaters.

text_translated_detailed: Mattau had placed itself under the subjection of the Dutch nation, whereupon it served them well. Then the most culpable among them brought themselves to us so that we might speak with them about this matter, which happened shortly thereafter, and they brought the most troublesome and guilty parties to us. After we had obtained good information about everything, indeed even their own confessions from these same people, we held them quite firmly, with the announcement to the entire community that we had come only to punish the wicked and not the good. Consequently, we would burn and raze only the houses of the evildoers. If they now preserved their houses from fire, they should bring water in reserve with them. The Commissioner was to keep this, which they accepted with the presentation of the wicked, hacking their own houses to pieces, with the promise to conduct themselves henceforth as good and faithful subjects and to acquit themselves accordingly. Thus, on the 9th and in the afternoon, after we had set fire to and razed various houses of these murderers, we departed again with seven of these principal offenders to Sinckan, where the next morning, after we had arrived with the troops, we had these seven prisoners—as long as the Company still maintained order—executed by beheading in the presence of all the inhabitants, to set an example among these brutal heathens. This accomplished, in the afternoon two or three of the principal instigators of the aforementioned Soelang came to negotiate peace with us. We had the points and articles upon which those of Mattau had been received in grace presented to them through Dominie Juni, so that they might lay these before their entire community. And if they approved of this, then within a few days they should appear at the Castle to make the surrender of their land and their lords' states.

text_translated_detailed: 5 A 5 23 Esteemed and most wise Excellency, and very gracious Lord Governor-General Antonio van Diemen, and the Esteemed Council of the Indies. During the past southern monsoon, dispatches have arrived here directly from the coast as well as from Siam, Quinam [Quanzhou/Fujian], and the Moluccas, together with very pleasant letters and accompanying documents (God be praised) dated at various times, which have arrived safely, and their loaded cargoes have appeared both here at the roadstead and in the Pescadores [Penghu Islands] as follows, namely: On the 20th of June last past, the fluyt ship Schagen arrived in the Pescadores, and on the 25th of the same month with an Esteemed letter dated the 16th of April last past, it arrived here at the roadstead. Subsequently, it proceeded inward with an anchor, and the remainder on the 21st of July, approximately one and a half miles south in sight of the coast on this side, was lost. The yacht Daman, sent over Quinam by the President Couckesack with Esteemed letters dated the last of May, and his Excellency's letter dated the 30th of June, likewise entered inward on the same day with the yacht Wateroo from the Philippines with a letter from the Esteemed Commander Engels dated the 13th of July. At that time, the yacht of the other ships, Wassenaar, the galeas, and the Exel, around the point of Cancoja (while making their way to the Pescadores), had separated. The aforementioned three ships arrived on the 19th in the Pescadores without encountering any enemy vessel at their designated anchorage around Cabo del Spirito Santo [Cape of the Holy Spirit]. text_translated_detailed:
Noble Gentlemen,

Whereas yesterday morning, as Your Excellency will see from the copy of the letter herewith enclosed from the first of this month, we have continuously experienced contrary conditions, with southerly winds at times and then again northerly winds with variable weather, and we have had a fire in the Channel, such that what we had hoped and resolved—that the yachts Daman, Hooch Caspel, and Kleijn Bredamme would be able to depart at their appointed time for their voyage to Giscadonis—could not be accomplished. This morning, when we obtained favorable conditions, the wind rose in such a manner that the said yacht could gain no advantage for its voyage in that direction, as it would first have to sail northward. For this reason, having taken counsel and found it good, we have deemed it best not to keep Your Excellency waiting any longer without some news from here. Instead, we have ordered the aforementioned three yachts to proceed their voyage with all possible speed directly to Batavia [modern equivalent: Jakarta]. In the meantime, we shall employ all possible means to convey the letters for the ships Peael and Bommel to Giscadonis as conveniently as possible—the sooner the better. Because the tide proved so unfavorable, it was necessary to bring the yachts out of the Channel at night (with lanterns and beacons in the Channel). And since this morning we have not heard from the yacht Kleijn Bredamme, apparently driven further by the north wind, we have placed letters from the Honorable Joan van der Burch for the Kleijn Bredamme in the yacht Daman, hoping that the said Kleijn Bredamme will reach Your Excellency in safety.

In Fort Zeelandia, the eighteenth of October, 1636.

Your Excellency's obedient servant,
Hans Putmans

text_original: Copia Ede Erntfeste wijse zeer Genereuse Hren Waer dat wij op gisteren Morgen als VEde bij nevens gaende Copie van Miliue hier inevensgaende in dato 8=en stantij int breede sullen gelieven te beoogen Aen d' Ed H. r gouv. generael Ed Erentfeste Manhafte ende raden van India wijse voorsienige seer genereuse Heeren zoude hebben Soo als onse generale missive den 5. deses dubbelt gereet hadde, met oock die van onsen predecesseur omme met schip texel, d'Jachten daman, & Hoogcaspel ijder een te seijnden, ende de mijnen, met t' schip Bommel haer toe ende t' Iacht cleen Bredamie versproocken was te gaen, ten eijnde U.Ed. bij een vandeselve eerst aenlangende, sondet mogen weten den stant ende gelegentheijt deser plaetse, Item hoe dat naer t' vertreck der geseijde schepen ende Jachten noch in voorraet lagen, ontrent de 6 fluijten ladinge Mijlen vaderlants retoer, ende Coopmanschappen voorde zuijder quartieren, doch heeft den harden Pariabelen Noorden Wint verhindert, dat niet eerder als den 8. deses hebben connen verseijlen, als wanneer het taijouans Canael tot bedaringe wat scheen aente stellen, welck hapgendat waer namen ende ordre gaven, bij ijder Baecken een Chinees mondt des champantgen met eenlichter geleijt wierde op dat de Jachten damanhoogcaspel ende cleen Bredamme, smorgens ten t uijren uijtloopen mochten, als oock geschiet is, t'jacht Bredamme soo haest als buyten t' Canael quam, heeft sijn reijse na costij laten voorstaen, sonder dat den oppercoopman Joannes vander hagendie de brieven aenboort brachte heeft ingewacht, dienvolgende V. Ed. deselve met Jacht daman toecomen onderwijlen sich een vliegende storm subijt verheffende, is gemelten vander Hagen op daman blijven staen, de loges boot hem weder na landt begevende, is voorde soulte revier verdsoncken een man verdroncken, ende d'resterende menschen hun met swemmen aen landt gecalveert dit verdrijven van gemelten vander hagen comt gants qualijck, alsoo hem
text_translated_detailed:
Copy

Noble, Esteemed, Wise, and Most Generous Gentlemen,

Whereas yesterday morning, as Your Excellency will see from the copy of the letter herewith enclosed, dated the eighth, we shall be pleased to lay out in detail for the Honorable Governor-General and the Esteemed, Honored, and Wise Counselors of India, most generous gentlemen, what we would have done, just as our general letter of the fifth of this month, prepared in duplicate, as well as those of our predecessor, in order to send with the ship Texel the yachts Daman and Hooch Caspel, each one separately, and mine, with the ship Bommel, to go to them, and the yacht Kleijn Bredamme was promised to go along, so that Your Excellency, upon the first arrival of one of them, might be informed of the condition and situation of this place. Item, how after the departure of the said ships and yachts there still lay in store, concerning six fluyt-loads of goods for the return to the Fatherland and merchandise for the southern quarters, yet the harsh and variable north wind prevented us from setting sail before the eighth of this month, when the Taiwan Channel seemed to calm down somewhat. Upon perceiving this, we gave orders that with each beacon a Chinese guide of the champagne [uncertain: original term] with a lighter escort be placed, so that the yachts Daman, Hooch Caspel, and Kleijn Bredamme could depart in the morning at the appointed hour, which also happened. The yacht Bredamme, as soon as it came outside the Channel, proceeded its voyage toward the coast without waiting for the chief merchant Joannes van der Hagen, who brought the letters on board. Consequently, Your Excellency will receive the same with the yacht Daman. Meanwhile, a sudden flying storm arose, and the said van der Hagen remained on the Daman. The lodge's boat, returning to land, sank in the salt river; one man drowned, and the remaining men saved themselves by swimming to land. This loss of the said van der Hagen comes very badly, as otherwise we would have employed him in the trade with Quinam with the Portuguese ducats, but now we must send another. The said van der Hagen was also commissioned to bring with a young man one of my minor letters to Bommel and another from my predecessor to the rear of the Caijonan, to the Governor Han Putmans, to the Honorable General, so that with these they might advance their voyage from the Pescadores to the coast. With this flying storm, the fluyt Warmont (which had laid its beams and redoubt in Wancan and lay under the north reef) was also driven from its place. Item, the yacht Waterloose Werve, loaded with lime from Wancan, both were driven from their places, such that it would come very badly for the Company. Should the chief officers of Warmont and the yacht Waterloose Werve proceed their voyage toward the coast, which we do not hope, yet if the same should happen, they would merit being deported together, not being worthy to serve the Company, for which sufficient reasons, in that they cannot stop again along the coast of China for their defense, will not bring forth. On the spot, we are sending people to Tancoija and Tamsuij to inquire whether they are staying there or thereabouts, and to give orders how best they shall proceed. These packets go with the under-merchant Ian Hendrixz Cracauw, over Mattauw, so that they come to Wancan, and to obtain a junk there, with which to cross over to the Pescadores, and to bring letters to both Texel and Bommel.

text_translated_detailed: The fleet continued sailing until the 10th of that month, when we passed by the places Pisang, Tinghij, and Babij, and toward evening we drifted in calm waters, being four miles from Poele Tijamon [Pulau Tioman]. At that point the captains of the respective ships informed us that their water supply was not as abundant as they had calculated it would be, and that the Chinese could scarcely manage with one small canoe of water per day. Furthermore, the Breedamme, the fluyt [merchant ship] the Swaen, and the yacht Hooch Caspel required timber work to make anchor stocks from, which could not be obtained in Batavia, for although we had anchors, we lacked the stocks for them. Since the General Company could not properly make use of them in case of necessity, and since these same stocks were also needed for the preservation of ships, lives, and goods on such a bare coast as Formosa [Taiwan], we found it advisable in council to run ashore on the west side of Poele Tijamon and to anchor in twenty-eight fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 51 meters]. There the ships were supplied with water, timber, and firewood with all haste, so abundantly that we departed again from the said Poele Tijamon with the aforementioned fleet on the 11th of July in the morning. Furthermore, the Breedamme, the fluyt merchant ship the Swaen, and the yacht Hooch Caspel required timber work to make anchor stocks from, which could not be obtained in Batavia, for although we had anchors, we lacked the stocks for them. Since the General Company could not properly make use of them in case of necessity, and since these same stocks were also needed for the preservation of ships, lives, and goods on such a bare coast as Formosa Taiwan, we found it advisable in council to run ashore on the west side of Poele Tijamon and to anchor in twenty-eight fathoms approximately 51 meters. There the ships were supplied with water, timber, and firewood with all haste, so abundantly that we departed again from the said Poele Tijamon with the aforementioned fleet on the 11th of July in the morning. I ordered the skipper not to go beyond bounds but to remain in the boat with regard to their resistance until some of the principal Portuguese had been subdued. The Portuguese were held back for the next dispatch by our men. Our men had scarcely come aboard when they were welcomed by the Portuguese, who willingly, upon the assurances we had made, handed over their ship and loaded goods into our hands, and transported themselves to our ship. From this I informed myself of the goods loaded in the yacht and with what cash it was provided. Captain Cosimo de Cardoso served us in answer that this yacht was loaded with nothing other than merchandise and carried no cash, because the merchants would suffer great losses in Macao from that. However, Father Alberta Polacq had approximately 350 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: a currency unit], and each of the others was provided with ten to twelve Rixdollars in cash. For this reason I immediately transported myself to the captured prize, both to secure for the Company the aforementioned cash and the goods lying at hand outside the hold, as well as to hand over the remaining Portuguese and Bengali slaves and to distribute them among our ships. text_translated_detailed: And more years are daily instructed by the said Junio in school in the way of life in the Sincanese language through Latin written letters. They are increasing greatly and are wholly eager to come to school. The young girls are also brought there by their mothers at the proper hour. About sixty girls are also daily instructed in prayers and otherwise catechized. The Sundays are not properly observed, and the sermons are heard by well over seven hundred people. There also, together with Junio and some Dutchmen, the schoolboys sing edifyingly before and after the sermon in the Sincanese language in the manner of the one hundredth Psalm of David. May God the Lord bless this good work and cause it to grow more and more. A village called Tavacan, located half a mile from Sincam, has been provided with the person of Cornelis Agricola, a sick-visitor [uncertain: original term for a pastoral care worker], whom we understand exercises himself well in the language and the foundations of Christianity, and likewise applies his zeal to sharpen the inhabitants of that village (who show themselves very willing) and to open to them the door of light. Furthermore, two villages lying to the south of Sincam, likewise Baccluangh and Maghinam to the north of Sincam, as well as those previously in the mountains, which has twenty-one villages under it, have likewise resolved to take up the true service of God and to abandon their superstitious practices entirely. So too do the seven villages of Pangsoija, which are very rich in people, especially in children. To the villages of Mattauw and Soulangh, likewise the seven Taccaranese villages and Lanckzouw, being fifteen villages, with yet eight villages lying to the east of Tacquenejangh, there is also good prospect that all will be drawn to our religion, which our predecessor and the said Junio fully affirm to us. So we also confirm with the opinion of Dominie Junio that there is quite a bit of improvement among these heathens.

text_translated_detailed: To the Esteemed Governor-General and Council of India, Your Excellency, most esteemed, valiant, wise, and most generous gentlemen: The foregoing is a copy of our general dispatch dated the 5th of October last, which Your Excellency, with the yacht Daman, [will receive] from Taijoan's canal, and also via the Piscadores with the ship Bommel, and another [dispatch] of the 9th of October via the ship Texel, which we hope Your Excellency will have received well before this, and the five ships and yachts with their loaded goods will have arrived safely. Regarding the incoming [news], we are pleased to report that the fluyt Warmont, which on the 8th [of this month] lay at anchor under two anchors beneath the northern reef, was driven away in the flying storm that came. When the anchor cable of one of its anchors broke, and the daily anchor dragged after it and would not hold, it was driven down to below Tancoija, remaining then in fear, because it was provided with no more than two anchors. The officers might easily have let it proceed along the coast, and thus would have deprived us of the forty beams and quantities of lime that it carried, and would have caused such damage to the Company that we would have been able to send a fluyt's cargo of return goods to the Fatherland at lesser cost, and there would have remained [goods] here. Regarding this, Your Excellency wrote that those of such rank and quality should be deported, since the aforementioned officers could not provide Your Excellency with sufficient reasons why they could not have prevented it again. Thus the aforementioned officers would have deserved such punishment. But since the contrary was done, and the proper measures were taken at hand, whereby also on the 12th of October [the ship] came up and entered the canal, namely at the land of Tancoija, where anchor ground is, where it with a northerly storm made an upper wall.

text_translated_detailed: He also declared that the order which the Viceroy of the King had over his ships consisted in this: that he must maintain all of the King's galleons and carracks in Goa in a clear and battle-ready state, so that when the opportunity presented itself, our forces being separated from the others and divided over a portion of Taiwan, then with good advantage one could attack the same in order thereby to bring their fallen state somewhat to redress, and to make their power formidable before the Indian Kings. This is what, Your Honour, has been communicated to me by the aforementioned Italian, and although I believe he has done much more, both because he would have been released from the captivity of the redoubt Seeburg, and because he communicated the same to me in service of the Gurle Compawas, so I mention this solely in order that what may be conjectured by Your Honour might be true, to serve Your Honour therewith, and to take the rest as spoken by a captive man. The advice regarding the chestnut brown horse brought over by us with Breda, and projected by Your Honour to be sent as a gift to Japan, became very sick on the voyage and against the departure of the fleet ships Swaan, Schagen, and Huijsduijnen heading there, and became completely unseen, not without great peril of dying on the voyage. For which reason we have had it remain at Saccam, with the Company's horses, in order to refresh it, until the next year's dispatch there, or unless Your Honour in the coming south monsoon should be pleased to order otherwise. The village Wavorolang, of which I make mention in my general dispatch, in that it has risen up against us, the matter concerning this has been taken into further consideration by our predecessor, and deemed good by the council to commit the Lieutenant with fifty soldiers to examine their situation, so that conveniently, as some thought, with two sincanders [uncertain: type of vessel] that had knowledge of the way, it could be done by water in order to resolve upon the findings of matters thereupon, in what manner one might attack the same with the help of our subjects and bring them under our obedience, this Savorolan being a village of the Lord Vanarnel, where not only many heartfelt [uncertain: possibly "hart-vellen" - animal hides or hearts] fall but the villages lying nearby also give much, those who must pass through there, and in war remaining would the supply in the aforesaid village be able to be cut off, which must be prevented by the best means.

text_translated_detailed: Upon this the aforementioned lieutenant returned on the thirteenth of October past from the said village to report that no proper access to the situation by water could be found there, having encountered a salt river to the north of Wancan where so little water was present that with the champans [modern equivalent: small flat-bottomed boats] they could not pass except at the highest water, and this so slowly that they had spent three to four days and never advanced so much that the redoubt in Wancan could be lost from sight, and when the way then came out into the sea, where the current showed itself in such a manner that he resolved rather to turn back than to pass through the same danger with such a foreseeable peril, whereby it became sufficiently clear to us that the water expedition was not feasible for us, and consequently it would have to be done by land. Upon which our predecessor and the council took the matter into further consideration, so as not to make a mistake, and to undertake this expedition with certainty, or whether the same should not be postponed until the five ships, namely Noordwijk, Iudewater, and the flutes thereof, namely Schagen and Huijsduijnen, should appear here or in the Pescadores from Japan, which we all equally have to expect, when then so much seafaring folk could be laid from the ships onto the fort and the redoubts, and consequently more soldiers could be lightened, so that two hundred soldiers could be made up for this coming expedition. But on the other hand, considering that then all the folk, both soldiers and boatswains, would be needed for the loading of the three flutes (with sugar and porcelain for the Netherlands as otherwise), Taijonan, Putmans to the Lord General, dated the tenth of October, it was therefore resolved: In case the aforesaid five ships should appear together before the fifteenth of November coming from Japan, then the said expedition from Wavorolang with the help of our subjects from Pangsoija, Mattauw, Soulang, and Sincans would be undertaken by land, and the same would be effected with little expense and less trouble than by sea, but if the aforementioned five ships should appear so soon and then appearing after the fifteenth of this month, the said expedition would be held in readiness until further support.
