And on the subsequent voyage, the news of Japan had reached the ears that the Mandarins of Siam had murdered their King, and the one now reigning, who had previously been merely a servant, had seized power for himself by force. For this reason, he was regarded by his Imperial Majesty and the council of Japan as an evil and treacherous people, because such treachery had been committed against their King. Moreover, a certain letter going herewith, written by the captain and interpreter of the Chinese in Nagasaki, to various Mandarins in Siam, tells how this nakoda, being simple and ignorant of the situation there, was not admitted to trade. But his merchandise, having already been brought ashore, had to be loaded immediately back into his junk, and he had to return to Siam without accomplishing his business. Since he had arrived here so opportunely, he requested to come hither from Wancan with his junk, to help sell his merchandise, to proceed to exchange it for Chinese goods, and to return to Siam as quickly as possible. His junk was loaded with 640 to 1,490 piculs of sappanwood, which would be worth here at 2½ rixdollars per picul, 3,500 guilders; 500 piculs of deer hides at 14 rixdollars per hundred, 70 guilders; 50 piculs of tin at 6 rixdollars and 5 stuivers per picul, 300 guilders; 4 piculs of elephant tusks at 50 rixdollars per picul, 200 guilders and 40 stuivers. In short, these goods being brought would amount here to the sum of 4,020 rixdollars

text_translated_detailed: In order to encourage the merchants to bring the silk to Amoy and so that we might receive a large quantity of fine silk coming in, we have also, in conformity with Your Excellency's good intention, raised the price of the silk with the merchants, according to the promise made to Taijonan dated the 10th of October by our predecessor, the last voyage made, namely those of 139 tael we had previously paid 140 tael per picol, those of 143 tael per picol we gave 144 tael. And we find, in proportion to the most recently received silk of this lot, to be even more beautiful and more even in thread, without the slightest defect, better than the previous, so that with the raising of one tael per picol, the Chinese will be encouraged to bring good silk, which will undoubtedly be of good service to the Company, as we observe both in the homeland as well as in Japan, the greatest profit comes from the finest silk, so we shall take this into account in the coming year to obtain a good quantity of fine silk, in order to bring the most profit to the said Company, which our predecessor has seriously recommended to us along with other good matters. text_translated_detailed: Most Esteemed, Mighty, Generous, Wise, Provident, and Discreet Lord General. The enclosed is a copy of my most recent particular letter dated the 8th of October last, sent from Wanckan from the Pescadores by the ship Texel, which I hope will have reached Your Excellency before the receipt of this, and the five ships and yachts will have arrived safely at the coast, which we shall be pleased to learn in due time. Since then we have watched with great longing every day for the two Chinese junks from Jochoo and Jockruij, which according to long-standing rumor were said to be loaded very expensively with approximately 500 to 600 [uncertain: possibly piculs, a unit of weight] of raw Chinese silk, various silk fabrics, and other goods. text_translated_detailed: According to the opinion of Captain Hambuan, undertaking any hostile action to obstruct the Chinese trade would be of such great consequence that it would be unworthy to resign ourselves to such a small matter. I therefore humbly request that Your Excellency be pleased to give the matter of lightening the pepper from the departing junk bound for China more careful consideration, and to set aside what has passed as a sign of what fruits it can bear, so that if Your Excellency finds the neglect to be most advisable, you would nevertheless be pleased not to give orders contrary to the ship's instructions to the captains of the ships, so that all misfortunes and causes of irritation that might befall the rich Chinese trade would be prevented and the trade preserved for the Company. We therefore wish to trust that my advice will be received by Your Excellency as fatherly and with paternal kindness, as I find it in my judgment to belong to the service of the general Company from the heart. With this, the most earnest, valiant, generous, and most discreet provision, may God pray that Your Excellency be preserved in good health and long life, and grant Your Excellency a fortunate, prosperous, and desired governance. In Fort Zeelandia, the 14th of November, 1636. Your Excellency's obedient servant, signed Johan van der Burgh.

text_translated_detailed:
Balance: ƒ 235,857. 6. 1 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders, shillings, and pence]

To the Honored, Esteemed, Valiant, General, and Wise, Foreseeing, and Most Generous Gentlemen, the Council.

The foregoing is a copy of our latest [letter] to Your Excellency, sent with the Bredamme and the fluyt Warmont yesterday evening, at which time I promised the Governor Putmans that this morning I would send the fluyt Schagen to follow (to which three hundred canassos [uncertain: possibly a type of sugar measure] of sugar, its water, and some provisions were still lacking), with which we were occupied day and night in order to complete the aforementioned effect. These then are the reasons why I have had this latest general missive written by two hands, so that in case the Schagen arrives before the Bredamme and Warmont, since our latest [letter] was sent with the five yachts and ships on the 8th and 14th of October last, Your Excellency would not lack advice. Accordingly, the same is amplified with these few rules, as Your Excellency must expect further writing with the ship the Galliasse, which will follow as soon as it is able. And so that Your Excellency may have knowledge of what has been shipped in the Bredamme and Warmont, in case this fluyt ship Schagen reaches the aforementioned two ships, enclosed herein is the copy of the invoice and bills of lading of the ships Bredamme and Warmont loaded with the following, namely: 22,123 catties [modern equivalent: approximately 1,331 kg] of white raw Chinese silk; 76,076 pieces of various porcelain; 1,601,650 catties of white sugar; 55,970 catties of brown sugar; 4,740 planquins [uncertain: possibly a type of fabric]; 1,783 taels [modern equivalent: approximately 67 kg] of black gold; 12,000 pieces of brickwork with one [unit]; 35 pieces of Bengali slaves; 3 basins. Transport total: ƒ 235,857. 6. 1. Carried forward. Item, by this fluyt ship Schagen goes: 10,160 catties of white raw Chinese silk; 1,080 pieces of white double even pelings [uncertain: possibly a type of fabric] for the homeland which are good; 257,100 canies [uncertain: possibly a measure] of white powdered sugar; and 20 Bengali slaves, untaxed. 86,261. 7. 8 [modern equivalent: guilders, shillings, pence]. Our latest [letter] to Your Excellency was sent with the fluyts the Swan, Schagen, and Huisduinen, dated the 15th of August last, which I hope will have arrived there with favor before the receipt of this, and Your Excellency will have received the same, wherein I advised you of what had passed regarding our voyage and as specified therein, how on the 29th of July, at the latitude of 22 degrees and 22 minutes, around four o'clock in the afternoon between Macao and Lamoa, we had seen four ships which lay with their sails set, watching, and we thought they were our ships. text_translated_detailed: Copy. 3rd of July. Since the Commander through the skippers of the 75-day register kept by the Commander Jan van der Burgh, Councillor of the Indies, during the voyage that with the Ship Bredamme [Breda:], on the 3rd of July in the year 1636, in company with the fluyt [flute-ship:] the Swaen [Swan:], and the yacht Hoogcaspel departed from the roadstead of Batavia [Jakarta:], in order to advance the journey to Taiwan [Tayouan:], in the morning around nine o'clock we sailed from the roadstead of Batavia with the land wind, set our course north-northeast, in order to run east of the islands of Ontough Java [Untung Jawa:], and as soon as we had passed the unrest, we formed a Council of War from the chief officers of the aforementioned ships, where all matters that might occur would be handled. We found it good to establish an equal order, that is one pound of rice for each man per day. Likewise two days per week, meat and bacon to be given, namely three-quarters of a pound of meat for each man and half a pound of bacon as before, for each man per week, likewise half a mug [mutsgen:] of oil and an equal half mug of vinegar for each man per week we shall give, in order that our provided provisions may stretch as needed. And in order to conserve our water we shall also give a ration of one flask [flapcanne:] of water to each man per day. Each ship and yacht received a letter from us, so that as much as possible we might remain together. We further arrested according to our provided instructions to sail east of the islands of Banca [Bangka:] and handed over the two packets of letters from the Honored Governor General and the Council of the Indies to the Governor Putmans in Taiwan [Tayouan:], and the Honored President Nicolaes Coackebacker in Japan, holding to the skipper of the fluyt [flute-ship:] the Swaen [Swan:], in case the others should come to be separated, and before we reached the roadstead of Tayouan [Taiwan:], our predecessor, the honored Governor

This yacht remained loaded with the following slaves and merchandise until July. Since the Commander was informed by the skippers of the 381—which was reported to me by the clerk according to his kept accounts—namely 228 slaves and slave women, among which were counted 20 Goanese lascars [Indian sailors], who served the Portuguese as boat's mates for their wages. 152 packs, both large and small, with putchuck [a fragrant plant]. 5 vats with incense. 19 to 20 packs of cloth, both large and small, in which according to rough calculation were valued at ƒ 2 [Dutch guilders]. Corge [uncertain: possibly a type of cloth]. 16 pieces of sailcloth or canvas. 5 ditto with Negapatnam textiles. 5 thomp [uncertain: possibly a type of cloth]. 10 pieces of tape. Carassende [uncertain: possibly a place or type of cloth]. Str [uncertain] wood. And the rest of Negro cloth, Negro packs, both large and small, 21 to 22. On hides in various small packages, of which the quantity remained unknown to them. Debv [uncertain]. 1 pot of rosewater. 2 pots of Massangh de saacque [uncertain]. 8 small packages of catechu [an astringent extract]. 2 packs. 2 elephant tusks. 1 sack. 1. 2 packs of cardamom. 18 pieces, both broken and made chests, made of Cochin wood. 76 pieces of caliver [musket] wood. 4 picol [modern equivalent: approximately 60 kg] of pepper. 15 small vats. 1 pot of olive oil. 14 small pots. 2 small vats of salted mangoes. 2 palanquins [sedan chairs]. 9 cables and ropes of coir [coconut fiber].

text_translated_detailed: To come sooner to them, meanwhile being busy here as well. On the following day all four ships were under sail, and had thrown overboard whatever they could, such that it brought us into strange thoughts, what ships those might be. For considering that friends had no reason to run from us, yet because they showed their mainsails very high with 2 masts, each judged them too large to be galleons. Thus with our topsails, that is, topsails, against 2 glasses [a period of time, approximately 1 hour] before sunset we had approached them very hard. We disputed with the others what ships those might be. The skipper and several others persisted in the first opinion that they were no other ships than the aforesaid ships from Siam. Others said that the admiral, who let the flag wave (which we could not recognize because a Dutch ship was sailing before the wind, which chased the other 3 ships), others that they were Spanish ships, which, crossing from Luzon, had called at Macao. Others that they were the galleons that were ending their voyage from Macao to Japan. Such that the Portuguese could in no way believe it, because it was so late in the year, as we conducted the aforementioned discourse about this. We saw shortly thereafter some goods drifting, of empty chests, vats, pots, chicken coops, and water melons and otherwise of little value, which they had thrown overboard to lighten themselves. Whereby it became very clear to us that they were the galleons that were ending their voyage to Japan, and had departed late from Macao, because, as the Portuguese sustained, it must have begun to blow first. Item, that also we could have waited for the four frigates, which we had seen on the 18th of this month, where the Captain General of the voyage would also have come. Thus being assured of this, and now the sun had already set.

In the afternoon the wind southwest with fair and clear weather, we sailed along the coast towards Tayouan, shortly after this the aforementioned wind became so violent that we were forced to come away from the coast and go around to the south, and it was difficult enough to sail above the Golden Lion Island and the mainland coast, thus having gotten somewhat into the sea, we shot our sails to be able to withstand the storm so that we only held two small topsails. Same day the wind variable, with rain and hard squalls, but we still saw the fluyt the Swan and our [ships]. Same day the wind southwest with fair and clear weather, we sailed with the ships Bredamme, the fluyt the Swan, the yacht Hoogcaspel, together with the prize small Bredamme (which had been caught by the storm several times before) came to anchor on the roadstead of Tayouan, our predecessor the Governor Putmans and friends there, and also found the Chinese trade very opulent, we found Chinese junks within the canal at anchor, which six from the coast of China had arrived with various merchandise, may the Almighty be praised for our safe and prosperous voyage, and also the aforementioned Chinese trade on Formosa. — 6th of the same month. From one pistol, Staensleer, 7 hides, 16 fine quilts, 8 taffeta cloths, 6 celas, 28 Saracen cloths, 8 pieces of petas and aritchodes, 12 pieces of their giellams, 3 pieces of white quilt quilts, 2 pieces of idle betillies or poor quality Cassé Bengale, 1 piece of their white basta, 2 white Tharems, 5 pieces of their true betillies of 24 asta wide, 1¾ ell, ten for 17 reales, 15. In a cloth, 21 pieces of Caramel of Amber strung together with the other, 7, 20 thereof somewhat smaller, 11 pieces of Angelis deiten, 1 piece of Crystal de montagne, 2 glass handles useful for seals, 13. Note one Hambuam, a portion of red lac, 5 pieces of boxhorn, 2 pieces of rhinoceros horns, one small coffer of amber very nicely made by a Dutch craftsman standing in its case, therein placed watches of copper gilt, one chain of glass decorated with gold thread bound together, 3 diamond rings, one silver spoon and 2 knives with the same handles, 30 pieces of black amber, 3 pieces of gum lac. The other canasters therein 1 cergie or 35 pieces

On the 14th, four junks arrived, of which three were from Aimoij [uncertain: local place name], one loaded with a quantity of porcelain, the other two with salt and rice as well as some roof tiles and a quantity of planks for sugar crates. The fourth from Pehouw [uncertain: local place name] was loaded with salt. The wind turned. text_translated_detailed: Sinckan appeared, reporting that he had been well received and entertained by the chiefs there, and that our intention together with this gift had been offered and presented to him, whereupon they had given answer: if the Dutch desired peace with him, he had nothing against that, but if not, that it was also good, whereupon the Chinese pressed him and made it understood that it was necessary that he enter into peace with us or that he still feared our power in the future. Against this the chief replied that we could not well climb the high mountains. But if we did so and were powerful enough, then he would be willing to go and climb even higher mountains. Finally, through the good reports which the aforementioned Lamphack made of the Dutch, it seemed that he gained more favorable feelings toward us, alleging that first a Dutchman, which they nor their forefathers had ever sought, would be welcome, and that then the gift would first be accepted. Some of his people were willing to come with Lamphack here and thus make a firm alliance. The brother of the chief seemed very inclined to come here with Lamphack, but was prevented by the principal, who was against it, notwithstanding the Chinese offered their persons and goods to be left in hostage. But it is the opinion of Doctor Junius that if one or two Dutchmen appear there, that the 16 villages of Longjau, which were previously mentioned as being of 18, of which 2 have been driven away by themselves, shall come to our friendship. To enter into peace with these people is not only necessary because the seashore on the east side of Formosa would be a stretch of weeks for us and the Chinese would gain freedom, in consideration that the Chinese who trade on the east side of the mountains are always constrained by the inconvenience of the roadstead, so.

text_translated_detailed: Many cried out and called to speak, so that we could make our intentions known to them thoroughly by this means. However, at Taijoan we could not get anyone who was willing to speak with us. Nevertheless, since we are of the opinion to undertake another closer attempt, we crossed over again. On this dispatch, there was written in response while we were still there that our forces would immediately transport themselves back to the aforementioned Golden Lion Island and fortify themselves there at the already designated place, well fortified against the enemy, so that by all possible means we could damage the same—whether with their cannons, or by making stinking smoke therein, or after that, since we are in the place and the matter is best known to us, we shall judge what is most suitable—to cause all destruction and bring it into our hands. And if we could not get water, we would supply them with clappis [a type of plant], which according to their writing are abundant there. However, since the great rain and hard wind mixed in with it, this dispatch could not be sent off that day but we were forced to hold the young messenger until the next morning. On the 26th of the same month, the weather was still rainy, so the enemy remained fairly quiet, such that the young messenger with yesterday's dispatches would depart for Tamsug. But since the rainy weather lasted two or three days and shows no sign of stopping, the Honorable Governor Outmans with the council took the matter of the Golden Lion Island into consideration with this foul weather and decided it was good to instruct the friends there that if they are still in Samoi upon receipt of this dispatch, or if they have been at the Golden Lion Island a second time and have returned there, they should immediately transport themselves back here with the continuation of this rain.

text_translated_detailed: Has lasted and shows no sign of stopping, so the Honorable Governor Outmans with the council, having taken the matter of the Golden Lion Island into consideration with this foul weather, decided it was good to instruct the friends there that if they are still in Samoi upon receipt of this dispatch, or if they have been at the Golden Lion Island a second time and have returned there, they should immediately transport themselves back here with the continuation of this rain and foul weather, the reason being that they could not then use their weapons against the enemy and the rain would easily cause much sickness among the people. However, on the aforementioned island, with good shelter from the rain and the enemy being established there (in order to gain greater reputation and standing with the inhabitants), according to the order also given, they should remain and by all possible means bring the enemy into their power. But if the weather becomes very fine and some advantage appears against the enemy, then they may undertake another closer attempt, provided that between the Honorable Governor and the council advice is given, what means there are to overcome our enemy or to enter into a contract with them, so that from here we may always be assisted with counsel and might. However, our people cannot yet perceive that they are inclined toward us (as the Esteemed Governor seeks to bring about) to settle near the wood-wanba [uncertain: possibly a place name or geographical feature] or some other place. It was also deemed good that the Esteemed Governor, in order to inspect the work in Wanckan once and to ordain what is necessary in proper form, shall do so at the first opportunity when the weather is good. Item, that a certain Lamey man whose mother (at the time when ours were still on the island) had rendered many services in various matters, shall on that account be freed and allowed to dwell in Sinckan [normalized: Xingang] with his mother, besides also fifteen or sixteen old men from whom the Company can expect no further service. text_translated_detailed: Hard cold and the Esteemed Governor Putmans arrived toward midday from Wanckan, having with him his Excellency the cashier and gunner, likewise everything that was necessary for the execution of the redoubt in proper form. On the 22nd not without difficulty the wind northerly with good weather. On the 23rd westerly wind and five junks arrived from Lissou with rice and little wood, likewise some spars and deck planks, with one of the mentioned junks we received a certain letter from the officer, head of the fluyt ship Schaagen, from which letter's tenor it was understood that the mentioned fluyt on the 20th of the month in the Pescadores in safety had been moored, and that from there it had again departed to continue its voyage here. text_translated_detailed: Mr. Roelof Couckebacker departed on the 6th with the ship Groot Wassenaer and galley, heading to Japan. The Almighty granted his Excellency favorable passage in good health. On the same day, a junk arrived from China, under the command of Aijmon, loaded with 1,506 piculs [modern equivalent: approximately 90,360 kg] of refined sugar. Another junk from Lizhou arrived with some 444 piculs of spars and deck planks. Likewise, one junk from Behouw arrived with little salt. The day brought northerly winds with good weather, and they continued as on the previous days to load the swan and schagen [types of vessels] with Japanese cargo. On the 12th, 13th, and 14th of the same month, the wind continued northerly. During these days, the loading of the aforementioned ships continued, and it was resolved that, God willing and the wind permitting, they would proceed on their journey to Japan tomorrow. It was also resolved that Mr. Couckebacker (since upon inspection it was found that there were not enough ships to transport all the cargo ready here for return to the fatherland) should arrange that as quickly as possible the three fluyt ships Swan, Schagen, and Huisduinen, empty except for silver and some small items, would be sent back here to bring the aforementioned return cargo from here to the fatherland in the greatest haste before the departure of the ships to the homeland. Furthermore, it was decided that his Excellency, for various reasons, would draw 200 taels [modern equivalent: a unit of currency] per deposit from the fluyt Vetten in Japan, so that here, to the great shame, damage, and detriment of the General Company, as is presently and in the future the case, we would not fall short of ready money. On the same day, the three fluyt ships Swan, Schagen, and Huisduinen departed outside the harbor's anchorage and at night with the land wind to proceed on their journey to Japan. The purchases mounted here total ƒ 725,836 and 18 stuivers [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders and stuivers, the currency of the VOC]. May God Almighty guide them all with favorable passage in safety. Likewise, two junks departed for Lizhou on the same day with westerly wind and good weather on the 16th of the same month.

text_translated_detailed: The yacht Daman was to be loaded first with good stone (as they had also completed on the 12th of this month when 4 junks arrived from China with 13 to 1400 piculs [modern equivalent: approximately 780-84,000 kg] of sugar, and it was resolved by the Honorable Governor Outmans and the council that as soon as the spring tide comes, the two yachts Bommel and Texel shall be sent outside to be broken up there with a portion of the goods, continuing toward the fatherland to gain time. Loaded and with Commander Engel, approximately 450 September 1638, Taijoan being clear, heading toward the Viscadores to anchor there and wait for the other ships to follow. From that day favorable wind. From a missive dated from the standing [position] in Wanckan from the upper merchant of The Hague, it was understood how certain overseers of the Chinese in Vovorolang had appeared on the 29th of August in Wanckan, relating how 180 to 190 Vovorolese had betaken themselves to Calk Island in flight in order, at an opportunity, to attempt something on the wooden fort Wambas there or indeed to set it on fire. Likewise, how since our made insinuation dated the 14th of February last past, the Chinese in place of being harsh now have many of their people treated well. This village Vovorolang would consist of 344 houses and approximately 1000 able-bodied men, with 400 of them under a certain Captain Sterk who would make [them ready] so that at an opportunity they could separate themselves from the others and come to dwell in Wanckan under our protection. The said Captain or overseer placed beforehand a letter at his house so that whenever something was attempted on this village by our nation, it might remain spared. Of all this, time was provided on the 14th of this month, not without having passed with variable wind and reasonable weather. On the same day, a junk from Rimoy arrived with 250 piculs of 15-pounder sugar, a portion of gold-thread and otherwise. Item, one [entry continues]

text_translated_detailed: Anthony van Diemen from the date of the 12th of November, ambassador and further attached papers. 459. Esteemed, Valiant, Wise, and Generous Sir. To the Honorable Governor General, My Lord, Your Excellency's very pleasant letter dated the 30th of May 1636 reached us with the arrival of the Honorable President Nicolaes Couckebacker under the island Champelo on the 25th of June following thereafter (with the ships Grol, Huijsduijnen, and Daman), and we were very pleased to understand from it that we had been provided with proper copies of instructions for the procurement or recovery of the 23,580 reales of eight [modern equivalent: Spanish silver coins] and rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] from the wrecked ship Grootenbrouck by the Honorable Governor Putmans, and it grieves us greatly that our commission in this matter has not been able to accomplish more. It is thus that we, following our instructions and insofar as knowledge from the Almighty has been granted to us, have neglected no diligence in this matter, but have worked everything to the best of our ability, which Your Excellency shall be pleased to observe clearly from the following. Our arrival, together with the Honorable Major Ariaen Anthoonisen, was on the 6th of March in the year 1636 in the Bay of Thoron, and after we had learned of the death of the old king and the resumption of possession by the young King in the trading place of Praijphoo, which had occurred within a few days as can be verified in our most recent letter sent on the 29th of March in the year 1636, we appeared again on board, and after an examination of the state of affairs there had been made, the aforementioned Honorable Major convened the Council and proposed that, considering we had received permission from the nearest Councilor of the King, we might freely land our merchandise (if we had any), for which suitable places had been assigned to us, or whether one should not, following this, although it was promptly contrary to our instructions, proceed thus, since the monsoon was mostly spent, such costly ships as the Grol and Warmondt on that same day, being the 13th of March, should set sail for Batavia—

The merchant Caser coming from land reported to the Honorable Major that there was still another junk and yacht expected at any moment, wherefore the unloading was driven so absurdly and hastily that according to our findings, from the ships Grol and Warmondt 39 bundles of Casiens or goods of 15 ostx unit of measurement each bundle were found to be short, as can be seen from the attached interrogatory and attestation, for as soon as the goods were in the barks, scarcely had I closed my letter to Your Excellency, and plunder was transferred, or if the goods were lifted and sails stood by, so that in the afternoon the ships ran to sea, where with fishermen's barks a portion of their officers, soldiers, and sailors who had guarded the goods had to be sent, therefore I firmly trust that Your Excellency shall be pleased to consider these attached copies of my previous letters from the date of the 12th of November past and further attached papers. text_translated_detailed: Triman. Having come before the King and having performed the proper reverence, he had us sit down after the old custom, at which time we presented to His Majesty with proper respect, in brief, the tenor of Your Excellency's letter, and likewise if there was anything objectionable therein, that we might be granted an explanation of the matter, in consideration of the fact that our Commander with his ships under the island of Champelo remained waiting for our return, who was expressly sent to settle all disputes in the best manner with His Majesty under proper conditions, so that we might continue to frequent trade in his land and the same remain unmolested from threatening evils. By what means this could be secured, we had no doubt that His Majesty could have understood thoroughly from Your Excellency's letter. The King answered that he had been able to understand the content of Your Excellency's letter very well, and therefore considered it unnecessary to repeat the same again. It would also be reasonable and just that Your Excellency recover the aforementioned 23,580 reales [reaelen: modern equivalent: Spanish silver coins], together with the cannons and further munitions that were demanded, but since he had never seen anything of it, much less enjoyed it, and everything had passed into his possession and he had brought the kingdom under his rule with weapons, he could not agree to any restitution. However, if Your Excellency wished to wage war in his land, he could not prevent it, for he lacked neither cannons nor power to resist. Without touching in the least upon the threat from Tonkin, but letting the same pass unnoticed, if Your Excellency would also be pleased to allow commerce to continue in his land, both would stand at Your Excellency's pleasure. Furthermore, they declared that if Your Excellency wished to allow trade in his land to proceed, that the same should first be pursued by no one other than us, but regarding the restoration of the 23,580 reales of eight, he could not agree, and would also not be approached about it anymore.

text_translated_detailed: 1243 ARCHITECT. These enclosed herewith are copies from my previous [letters] of the date of the 13th of November last past, and further regarding the enclosed papers. Papers of 1470. Missive from His Majesty the King of Quinam to the Dutch King. Since the 19th. I have read in the old records and found that the righteous Kings have their kingdoms to govern with light, and that they hold the entire world, or all nations far and near, as their friends and allies. My honored father and ancestor was a truly mighty King and Lord, maintaining peace and correspondence with the Dutch, not knowing that there were any wicked subjects of His Excellency or of the realm, but that Annembij, being a great officer, sought to pursue his private profit in this manner. So with the sending of the Dutch, the deceased King and my aforementioned honored father was very skillfully able to close his eyes, so that he neither saw nor had the slightest knowledge of it. However, I have caused the aforementioned Annembij to be punished for his wicked deeds with death, and had him cut into small pieces, as an example to many. Now it is that afterwards from the Dutch King a certain envoy has been commissioned to me, dealing with the differences that occurred before, and bringing me a gift, consisting of twenty pieces of silver, two pieces of cloth, forty rolls of damask, ten red silks, two robes, and two Corgie [uncertain: possibly a type of fabric or garment] silk clothes. For this I thank Your Excellency. I request that the King of Holland show his magnanimous and godly heart toward my father and me, in that the previous differences and disputes are no longer to be remembered, but on the contrary, with my beginning of governance, the friendship and correspondence in Quinam be renewed. Furthermore, I request of Your Excellency that it please [you] that all merchants, frequenting my land, both coming and going, of Your Excellency's subjects may conduct their trade unharmed and unmolested, so

text_translated_detailed: Regarding the enclosed papers, 485 weapons from a Letter of His Majesty the King of Quinam [Quinhon/Cochinchina] to the Dutch King, dated the 19th. In the third place, Almighty God. I have read in the old chronicles and found that righteous Kings have their kingdoms fall easily to govern, and that they hold the entire world or all nations, both far and near, as their friends and allies. My honored father and ancestor was a rightful and mighty lord and King, maintaining peace and correspondence with the Netherlands, knowing that there were some wicked subjects of his Excellency or of the land's lord, but that one of them, being a great officer, sought to pursue his private profit in this manner with the sending of the Netherlands. The deceased King and my aforementioned honored father knew very well how to close his eyes so that he neither saw nor had the least knowledge of it. However, I have caused the aforementioned officer to be punished for his wicked deeds with death, and had him cut into small pieces as an example to many. Now it is that afterwards a certain envoy from the Dutch King has been commissioned to me, dealing with the differences that occurred previously, and bringing me a gift consisting of twenty pieces of silver, two pieces of cloth, forty rolls of damask, ten red silks, two robes, and two pieces of Goanese cloth. For this I thank Your Excellency. I request that the King of Holland show his great magnanimous and godly heart toward my father and me, in that the previous differences and disputes should no longer be remembered, but rather on the contrary, with my beginning of governance, the friendship and correspondence should be renewed in purity. Another request to Your Excellency is that you be pleased to allow all merchants frequenting my land, both coming and going, who are subjects of Your Excellency, to conduct their trade unharmed and unmolested. If this is understood and followed by Your Excellency, then the friendship between Holland and Quinam shall certainly continue unbreakably.

Two. During our presence in Quinam, we learned from the Nachoda and others of a certain Chinese junk coming from Cambodia, which arrived there on the twenty-eighth of June past, how upon his departure from the River of Cambodia on the nineteenth thereof, the ship Oudewater had not been captured. Similarly, the Japanese junk of the year 1635, departed from Nagasaki with the Emperor's pass and remained there for a year (having come to Cambodia with the junk in exchange for one of greater burden of approximately six thousand picol [modern equivalent: approximately 360,000 kg]), with approximately one hundred thirty pieces of deer hides, a portion of roe deer hides, sack or siram, Cambodian nutmeg, and other goods to Japan on the twenty-fourth of May had set sail. This voyage will not only freely damage the General Company in her Japanese commerce, but it is also to be feared that the ship Oudewater, being unloaded, will be forced to abandon its destined voyage.

text_translated_detailed: on the 7th of March arrived in Nijcko. We understood from one of the Gentlemen of the Lord of Firando the great longing of his Excellency and the Councilman Tackimod toward the Dutch commissioner, just as upon his arrival on the 19th of the same month in Fedo [Edo], when his Excellency seemed pleased at his arrival, he was asked what had caused the long delay or late coming to court, although previously with good will and order from his Lordship to dispatch all the ships and to come up to the warehouses, it had been deferred to trust. However, with the answer on this matter and the order given through this, they held themselves entirely content. Among other reasons, his Excellency related the discontent of the Nagasaki governor toward the Dutch nation, which consisted in our bold, arrogant, fearless manner of living and trade, in that we did not respect the Majesty and his commands, nor the persons who ruled in his name, we did what came into our minds, and thereby boasted that our principals had commanded us thus, as if thereby to show that we wished to live both in Tappan according to the order of our Masters as well as in the manner of our quarters, and so forth. By the request or supplication of the five imperial cities, as well as of the Dutch, Portuguese, and Chinese, white raw silk was to be placed under lock and key and distributed among the elders and overseers of the aforementioned cities who were qualified for this. These unheard of and false complaints were attached and delivered to the Councilman Sannicked. However, according to the Councilman Tackimond and his Excellency, sustained as our other friends, the supplicants in their made request obtained nothing, but were flatly rejected. Wherefore the matter concerning our [interests] might be at rest and have no fear that the same would be thrown upon the Company's shoulders. I have merely given the decision rendered in my Instruction to the chief merchant Caron by humble remonstrance to request a portion of the raw silk for the five imperial cities, one [portion] through those of Firando, but the greatest or greater part to be retained for the Company. This was taken by his Excellency as a childish proposal and answered that, in case these people's request were granted, just as we do not doubt you mean to divide a thread of silk, and such being granted or spoken by the Majesty, it can neither by force nor by me and anyone else be sought, requested, or changed. Let the past of such and similar things be your teacher. In order therefore to support the supplicants as much as possible in their made request and to refute the false calumnies and charges with the truth, before the arrival of the commissioner, by his Excellency in the form of a letter to the Councilmen Sannicked, Gangad, Auwadonne, and Insdonné, dated the 7th of February, was written and delivered, whereby it was requested of their Highnesses that, in case they had resolved to establish new orders, as those given by the Emperor Gongensamma regarding the Dutch, that this might be done under reverence to his governor hastily. So likewise for the same purpose a certain written justification was set forth by his Excellency and signed by the chief merchant Caron and delivered to the Councilman Tackimond, which pleased him well, to be delivered in the

86 stuivers per ell [unit of measurement] totaling 747 guilders, 13 shillings, and 8 pennies, and it should be 797 guilders, 13 shillings—the difference of 50 guilders has been remedied here and thus recorded. text_translated_detailed: The Honorable President reports that without being able to accomplish or obtain anything, he had received his discharge upon his request to depart for Firando [Hirado], having enjoyed mostly reasonable weather during this period of eight days, so that, thank God, on the evening of March [date], he arrived safely in Osaka. Then we had the Treasurer of the Lord of Firando in Osaka request of the Regent of this city whether his Lordship would be pleased to consent that the Commissioned Hollanders on behalf of the Company might come to deliver their presents to his Imperial Majesty and the lords of the realm, and we received the answer yes. Then early in the morning we went with these presents, namely one piece of silk damask, three pieces of velvet, and two pieces of figured damask, to the aforementioned Judge's house, where we obtained an audience before his Lordship and were received very courteously. We accepted the gifts and he wished us good fortune on our journey. Coming to the house, we made preparations to repack the gifts, with which we spent the rest of that day. And it became clear, and we had accomplished everything necessary for our journey, likewise the woodworks had been contracted for and assigned, which the Honorable President had been instructed to purchase here. On the [date], it rained, though not very hard, wherefore we resolved to depart, which we did. Coming at midday to Fira Kata to hold our midday meal, it rained the whole day, yet we undertook the journey and arrived in the evening in Miako [Kyoto]. text_translated_detailed: in order to inform his Honor of our arrival here. On the 8th. On this date in the morning, rainy weather, we departed from Miako and undertook our journey in twelve days, much of the time rain and bad weather, so that we, thank God, arrived safely in Yedo on the 19th. Coming from the country road, we intended to go straight to his Excellency's lodging and present ourselves before his Honor, but we understood that his Excellency had departed twelve miles outside Yedo to the Falconry (to amuse himself) and had gone away, wherefore we went to our lodging. In the evening, late around nine o'clock, we learned that his Excellency had returned. We immediately went to his lodging, but could not come to speak with him, he excused himself greatly before us, saying that it was very late and that he would have us summoned tomorrow. We were welcome, etc. On the 20th. We went to the house of the Lord of Firando, where upon his Excellency's appearance we presented ourselves for the first time, saying we were glad about our arrival. He would immediately write a letter to the Councilor Tackimond and inform his Lordship of our arrival. He further asked how we had been delayed so long, what rarities we had brought for the Majesty, whether Captain Couckebacker had also departed, to which we answered that the inclination to come above earlier had been good, but since it had pleased his Excellency to allow it, we would freely and at our leisure first dispatch all the ships and then come above to pay our respects, which is what happened. We left him with the assurance that when at the time as we appeared here last year, we would be timely enough, which has now happened eight days earlier. Regarding the rarities for his Majesty, his Excellency took upon himself to present the liberation of Pieter Nuijts to the Majesty through the Councilor Hannickedr. The Governors of Nagasaki complained about the Hollanders over the Commissioned ones.

This same burgher had come (as he said) to visit us, apparently to feel our pulse, and asked us freely, among other reasons, what and what reason was it that we had refused to lend to his Excellency in his great need for money. He told me—he spoke to the Company's servants—with these words: "It grieves me that I approached the Dutch for a loan. I had humbled myself before them and made my request, and they have refused me, whereby I became all the more embarrassed, for I had relied upon them. And otherwise, being forced to fall back, I had to suddenly borrow money at unsuitable places, and at such high interest as is extraordinary." We answered that we were very sorry to understand such a thing.

83 Christians, namely men, women, children, old and young, crippled [people] were found. For these people, outside in the field, a palisade was made round about with bamboo and wood, high and dense, wherein the aforesaid 83 people with all that they had were placed, sitting under the blue sky, in the sun, rain, and wind, all around guarded with watch-posts strictly, so that no one might give them any assistance or speak to them, in order to know the same certainly. We would send a servant there who reported to us thus the truth to be, there being among them great wailing and crying, principally from hunger of the children, of which some had already died. The order concerning this is that none of their bodies may be buried before and until they have all died together from hunger.

On the 11th day, we went to learn whether anything favorable had occurred in our matters, to the house of His Excellency, to whom we recommended our matter as well as the reverence to be shown on the 15th. [He] answered us: "I shall not forget you, and the document of which I spoke to you recently, I shall attend to it with the first [opportunity]," with which we took our leave and returned.

On the 12th day, we went again to visit His Excellency and to present ourselves at his house, by whom we were called inside. His Excellency's written response showed us a document which he had thus composed to the Councillors against the calumnies which he sustained. The Councillors [found it] most pleasing, and it served well for the refutation of the lies and calumnies of the Company's servants thrown upon [his] neck, reading as follows:

The injustice has been presented to the Regents of Nagasaki [Nagasaki:], [claiming] that in April of the year 1636 in Yedo [Edo:], all our merchants this year were bought up by 20 persons, and our trade was conducted alone with 20 persons. And those who charge us with this are certain persons who have not dealt with us.

We rob the Chinese on the sea and are in fact nothing other than robbers. We say such [accusations] are untrue. In former times we were inclined to trade in the land of China. To this end and to request such [permission], we sent our commissioned ambassadors to China. Through them we were answered: "Foreign ships and people we do not allow in our land. However, if you wish to go with your ships to the island of Rougao [uncertain: possibly Rouquan or similar:], there we will trade with you and do business." On this promise, His Excellency found it good that the aforesaid document, although the Chief Merchant Caron wished to bring something against it, should thus be composed and delivered. April of the year 1636 in Yedo [Edo:], and [with] a concluded contract, we sent a good number of ships and a rich capital to the said Pehou [Penghu/Pescadores:]. However, we found that they dealt with us in all things very cunningly and deceived us with all manner of lies. Indeed, in place of granting us trade, they finally took our ships, money, and people, which they most shamefully burned and murdered. Since that time, in revenge and vengeance, we have taken some of theirs, whatever we could master, from them. Concerning this, those of China sent their ambassadors again to us in Jacatra [Jakarta:] with this address: "The island Pehou lies under the jurisdiction of China and consequently we may not tolerate foreigners there. But if you wish to settle on the island Formosa [Formosa:] in the harbor of Taijouan [Tainan:], we will provide you with everything according to your wish, the fullness of merchants." This contract, concluded anew from both sides, our trade with those of China has remained established until this day. Far from us and from what we are, we take or injure no one other than our open enemies.

text_translated_detailed: Island Formosa [Taiwan] in the harbor of Taijouan [Tainan], if you wish to establish yourself there, then we shall bring you the fullness of merchant's goods according to your wishes. Since the contract has been newly concluded on both sides, our trade with those of China has remained stabilized until now; far from us, and from where we are, we take no one else as our public enemies, or injure them. / 37th month, 7th day. To the governing gentlemen. From François Caron, a preamble or justification, which was read aloud to us by the writer, His Excellency asked what we thought of it. We answered that the substance regarding the matter of the Portuguese, as well as that of the Chinese, seemed in some way to touch upon the root of the matter, but that the explanation would have to proceed in quite a different manner. However, said His Excellency, I have thought it good to set it forth in this way, and that shall please the gentlemen best. You shall not be questioned further here, or further interrogated. Be content with that. We thanked His Excellency for all favor, and confirmed ourselves with what His Excellency had been pleased to set forth. Thereupon two such writings alone were drawn up and signed by us. His Excellency said: the one I shall keep with me at the required time, to show it sometimes to some great personages, and the other I shall hand over to Councillor Carkimond [uncertain: possibly Kakiemon or similar], so that through his honor it may be shown to the councillors at a more convenient time, and their dispositions may be favorably inclined toward you through such and similar matters against you. text_translated_detailed: —his honor might show at a more convenient time to the councillors, and their dispositions might be favorably inclined toward you through such and similar matters against you. We thanked His Excellency again, saying that we would not be negligent in showing all his good counsel and favor to the honored Lord General, and in writing to him. Also, we asked whether His Excellency would also find it inadvisable that in the written justification shown by His Excellency to Councillor Iacomond, which his honor pleased him with promises to show to the councillors, the Dutch were complained of, that they were burdened by unknown or unintelligent people, and that His Highness had promised to show this justification at a good time to the councillors in full assembly. — from the appearance before May, April, year 1636. In the aforementioned writing, another point might be added, namely the request for the release of Lord Nuits. In response to this, yes, in all respects I find that inadvisable, for if you begin to show written requests and hand them over, you will not know in how much time or how many months you will receive an answer to them. And without an answer you could not depart. This present writing is nothing more than a simple justification, which once read and reviewed, is thought of no more or asked after. On the other hand, I have resolved to speak for Nuits from my own person, and to say thus: governing gentlemen, not the Dutch, but I, my person it is, I request his release, for I have become compassionate toward this foreigner. Let his release be granted to me, etc. And I wish to try in this manner whether I can obtain his freedom. We confirmed ourselves in all things with the good counsel of His Excellency, and they departed. On the 13th, 14th, and 15th days, rainy weather, nothing else happened. We understood that Councillor Outader [uncertain: possibly Ōtada or similar], who had already lain sick for six months, was dead from illness. text_translated_detailed: The aforementioned councillors Gedde and Cangade had sent a letter signed by their three highnesses to Councillor Tackimond, of which I shall set forth the extract here below. On this date, His Imperial Majesty has granted that the foreigners on the 15th at the ordinary time shall do reverence. You shall send this order to Matsura Suckenoramij so that the law may be made known to them. To the castle at the house, the commissioned one is charged to return to their lodging and until the 28th day of April, year 1636. In Tido, His Excellency previously charged us that we should make everything clear that was necessary for the audience. We let His Excellency be thanked most highly and promised to comply with everything. On the 19th day, when we had made everything ready, two noblemen from His Excellency were sent to our lodging to inspect the gifts on the presentation boards and to see whether everything was in proper form and clear. These noblemen were also ordered to appear with us in the castle the next morning. Shortly thereafter, a nobleman from Lord Tackimond came with the charge from his lord that we should interrogate him regarding the copper crown with the palisade and all its appurtenances, maps, etc. This was done accordingly. The crown we had marked all over with Japanese letters so that no abuses would be committed by the Japanese. We would have the interpreter there as well, to learn how it would turn out with it. The aforementioned crown was brought into the castle, into the house of Councillor Tackimond. Two noblemen were commissioned to take it out and set it in, so that afterward in the palace no difficulty would occur with it. On the 20th day, in the morning with daylight, three noblemen came, one of them with the present horses, and two on foot, to guide us to the castle from Captain Sacqmond. We went together with the presents to the house of Councillor Tackionde, where we were charged to wait. The aforementioned noblemen, together with the interpreter, went into the inner palace, where they found the lord of Firando and Councillor Cackimond, and announced our arrival. Their honors charged us to wait until the most urgent and hottest matters would be over, and then they would have us summoned. After waiting an hour, the gifts and copper crown were summoned into the inner palace, which made us rejoice, and we also hoped we would soon follow. But after we had waited another two hours, we were told from the castle that we should return to our lodging. There was too much to do. We could not get a turn, for there were too many lords appearing at the audience at court. With this sober comfort we had to return. Shortly thereafter, Councillor Tackimondonno sent another messenger, through whom he let us know that we should leave the gifts just as they stood with all their equipment in his house until the 28th coming audience day. He wanted to take good care of it, which was done, and we returned home. On the 21st and 22nd days, nothing remarkable happened, rainy weather. Being as it were the father of May, these Dutch lost a harder favor, the commissioned one remained at the house of His Excellency to dine in order to be with some gentlemen from the castle—

text_translated_detailed: On the 29th we went to the house of the Lord van Firando [Hirado:], where we waited half the day before we could manage to speak with him. Finally he appeared and invited us to remain and dine with him, saying: "At a good time you have come here, gentlemen. This evening I have three high officers of the Company's affairs, or Regents from the castle, as guests, to whom you might also conveniently make known your matters." We thanked His Excellency for the friendly address and waited until finally the gentlemen arrived. With them we had indeed had acquaintance from earlier times. Their Lordships spoke to us very kindly, and our company seemed to please them greatly. They began to relate many new and strange worldly things and to ask questions, to all of which we could answer as best we could in a courteous manner and gave them satisfaction. Finally His Excellency spoke again while sitting, saying: "Alas, these people are unfortunate." Their Lordships asked how so. His Excellency answered: "They have come here for a simple audience and have already—I know not why—waited more than fifty days for it. Moreover, they have for so many years requested and begged for the release of the given Governor who sits imprisoned in my domain, that they have grown weary of asking and requesting. I must see whether I can obtain this request for myself." Their Lordships understood all this and said: "Certainly they are unfortunate. We cannot imagine how this might come about. His Majesty's order is nonetheless not such. We will hope that you will obtain it by the 28th audience." From these and similar reasons, together with firm promises of the 28th coming, the writing of the Council Cangado [uncertain: possibly Cangada or similar] to the Lord van Frando regarding the Netherlanders' audience will hold back the release of Your Excellency's Nuits in the College of Councilmen of the Netherlanders' situation.

text_translated_detailed: preparations toward Nicko [Nikko]. The Dutch received the ordinary gift of twenty robes of silk. May, Year 1636, in Iedo, on the 8th, we went to the house of the Lord of Firando to learn how matters had gone with the gifts to the Councillors. Arriving there, we understood that all the aforementioned gifts had been sent to each individually, but not one of them had accepted it, each giving as answer that if other Councillors accept it, I shall do likewise. However, out of respect for the Lord of Firando and his letters of recommendation, we did not send the gifts back, but left them in the keeping of their secretaries for further clarification of matters. We could not come before His Excellency, but His Lordship, having understood our situation, sent word to us: your gift is safely kept in good hands. I shall personally request Councillor Samikidonne in person to be pleased to accept this small present, which he will not refuse. Once this happens, all others will follow him in this. We thanked His Excellency and returned. On the 9th and 10th nothing particular occurred. We learned that His Excellency had written a letter of recommendation regarding our license to Councillor Tackimede, in which he showed him that we—were the ones who had to be present for the Company's ships in Firando, which time was already beginning to approach. And we waited for nothing else here but the license from His Majesty. In the evening we sent the Tolck [interpreter] to learn what answer had come regarding it, of which I here set down the extract. Your recommendation regarding the Dutch license, I have well understood. There is so much to do that such small matters cannot well find place. After that I shall present it to the Imperial Majesty tomorrow. On the 11th, the Lord of Firando sent us a messenger and had him inform us of the license to depart, and also that we should send the Colck [uncertain: possibly a variant of Tolck/interpreter] early tomorrow from the Castle to receive the ordinary gift from His Majesty given to the Dutch, and to hear the given word of license, that the Dutch shall depart again. On the 12th, early in the morning, the Tolck went to the Castle, where he was told by Councillor Tackionde that His Majesty, on yesterday, had granted the Dutch license to depart again. He also gave him a document to receive in the warehouse of the Commander thereof twenty silk robes, which all happened accordingly. After the Tolck had returned, we went to thank the Lord of Firando [because] the gifts had been accepted by all the Councillors. Arrival of the commissioners in Firando, May, Year 1636, in Iedo. We went to his house, who wished us good fortune over this good fortune and recommended us to depart at the earliest and wait for nothing more. The Lord Nuits, together with the Company's pending matters, he would keep in mind. Furthermore, he said: the day after tomorrow I wish to come to your place to eat a meal. Let Dutch food be prepared for me, for I have a taste for it. We thanked His Excellency for everything and took our leave.

Regarding the answer, they still had to consult with one another and arrange and write things, and as soon as they were ready, they would let us know. In our letters to the Lord of Firando, we recommended to His Excellency that, as he deemed it proper and advisable, some gift should be made to His Majesty's messenger or to the Council members as a token of gratitude. His Excellency was to understand that in such circumstances, he should be pleased to act in such a manner as he would find best to serve the contentment of the Japanese high authorities and the honor of the Dutch nation. The reasons why no gift would be sent with the Dutchman were these: First, that there were no goods presently available for gifting in the warehouse, but everything had been sold, and we did not know to whom, how much, and what had been given away. Therefore, we had been instructed to buy none in Macao, and principally also to know whether gifts had been made before, or whether they would be entirely discontinued by His Excellency. We therefore requested that His Excellency would be pleased to provide or have called for such goods in Edo as he would find necessary. In July of the year 1636, the assistant, namely Reijniersz, departed as Chief Merchant to Edo. He was called to the house to receive the letters that had come from His Excellency from Edo, as well as to hear the verbal and written instructions. The nobleman, being the messenger, had arrived.

text_translated_detailed: We have understood your reasons, and it is accepted as just by us, and that you do not willingly have the Dutch in your land has been brought to our attention by you many times before, and is also not unknown to His Majesty. However, since His Majesty allows the Dutch to remain in Firando [Hirado], we trust that you and your subjects might derive some benefit from this, which inclination you kindly maintain. And it is the intention of this council to hear from you henceforth what occurs in the Dutch matter, whether good or bad, and to receive from you all goods and rarities that might be brought by the Dutch and be useful to His Majesty. Moreover, the nobleman who had come from Zedo [Edo] recounted of his own accord that the Council's Excellency would have addressed him thus: we have also been advised many times to propose to His Majesty that he lay upon you the governorship over all foreigners, as well over Tsushima [Tsushima], Korea, Nagasaki as Firando, to which matter we are well inclined. To which his Excellency answered, regarding Firando, that must be, there I shall take patience, but the rest shall never be granted by me. I am a simple person and not fully capable of governing my own land and income promptly, what then should I undertake in such a wide situation? With that he took his leave. text_translated_detailed:
...heard nothing that day, although we were eagerly waiting, hoping that the Almighty would grant a good outcome.

On the seventeenth, Thursday morning, the wind was northeasterly with cold, clear weather. Seroshedon had been at the house of Tackemede and Sannikes Samma to advance our negotiation. Also His Majesty had gone hunting that day, so nothing could be accomplished. Toward evening I was summoned by the Lord of Firando. So he told me that he had induced all the Councillors and nothing else would be heard except that His Majesty must present the Request. In short, it was one and the same old door through which the complete discharge must take place. I requested a Dutch storm hat. On account of this I sent a letter to the Lord President, and the good people of Nagasaki had arrived.

On the eighteenth, Friday morning, the wind and weather were as before. Early on, the Lord of January, in the name of the Lord, 1636, in Gedou, the Emperor's castle of Japan, Stixando had ridden to the house of Sannike Samma to advance our trade. But today nothing further was heard.

On the nineteenth, Saturday morning, the wind was from the south, weather as before. The aforementioned Seroshedon came and reported that the Lord Tackemondon had spoken of our matter, so they now promised that the Lord Councillor Sannike Samma would press the matter and bring the trade to an end. For this it was necessary that it should happen within a short time, as it was well known to them that the last ships would soon depart. He promised to do his best.

On the twentieth, Sunday morning, cold, clear weather with sunshine. As was customary, I sent the interpreter to the house of the Lord of Fexando, as we had decided to send an express messenger to see if there was anything favorable to report about our business, and to press him further. I requested that I myself should go, as the last ship would have to sail within a short time.

text_translated_detailed: and we accomplished nothing to our sorrow. / First of February, Friday morning, the wind east had blown quite strongly. The interpreter was sent to the lord van Firando, and the aforementioned lord reported daily his activities and expected daily news with good hope. / 2nd, Saturday morning, the wind north with cold, damp weather. Seroskedon came to visit us. He had been with the lord's officer Sannickesamma. February, In the Name of the Lord, 1636. In Tedoue [Edo], the Emperor's Court of Japan. And our matter was heartily recommended. He promised that, as the Songuats, being their New Year's feast, would be on the sixth of this month, we would have a good outcome of the trade. / 3rd, Sunday morning, the wind and weather as before. We learned nothing on this day. That evening I understood through a servant of the lord van Firando that a letter from the lord Tackemond had come. He held it in reserve because there was no suitable opportunity. We would still present the matter of the lord Nuijts to his Majesty, but could not carry it through, and the Songuats could not conclude it. Therefore the Hollander could well depart. That night we packed our belongings. It began to rain this night. / 4th, Monday morning, the wind north with heavy rain. The horses were saddled. Meanwhile I went to the lord van Fixando, took my leave, and received gifts. Towards midday the young lord was presented with two Japanese robes as gifts, and we departed from Jedo [Edo] with a palanquin and five last of horses. [modern equivalent: approximately 10 tons] We passed through Snnangau. As the rain continued and the wind increased, we all got thoroughly wet. We led on to Gauwasackij. The rain continued that night. / 5th, Tuesday morning, the wind as before with a storm raging as before. We passed the high clayey mountain range, which was so steep that the horses were slipping and falling. The road was so bad that we had to stop in the village of Seka. The rain continued and a storm arose. We lodged in Fonsesan. We rode eight miles. Around midnight the rain began to stop. / 6th, Wednesday morning, the wind northeast with cool weather. Due to great flooding, the bridge was broken. We crossed the water with horses, saddled and bridled. From there, by the swift-flowing stream, which now ran with three channels, we crossed by ferry and led on into the city of Oudaulze, at the high mountain range Fauckonnij. Here each person had planted green branches and May flowers for their children, as tomorrow was their New Year or Songuats. / 7th, Thursday morning, new moon, the wind south with lovely weather. We had to depart early in the day because of the Japanese New Year. We rode towards the mountain range. We encountered a servant of the innkeeper in Hosacka with a gift sent to me, and so forth onwards.

text_translated_detailed: The city of Oudaulze [uncertain: possibly Odawara], at the high mountain range of the falconry, here each person had planted green branches and May flowers for their children, since tomorrow was their New Year or Songwats [uncertain: possibly referring to a Japanese New Year celebration]. On Thursday morning, New Moon, the wind from the south, with pleasant weather, we had to depart early in the morning on account of the Japanese New Year. We rode against the mountain range and encountered a servant of the innkeeper in Hosacka [Odawara] with a gift sent to me, and then went further to Jedo [Edo]. In the afternoon we rested in the Elecke falconry above; from there we rode off, the road was very deep and muddy. We arrived in the evening in Missima below the mountain range, having ridden eight miles. On Friday morning, the wind as before, with rough weather, we passed various waterways with horses. We rested in Josij waxe [uncertain]. From there we had a reasonable road. At the bank of the swift-flowing river we received letters from Hosacka from the express messenger. We crossed this river with ferries, which now with ice floes ran swiftly away. We ate our midday meal in Cambaer [uncertain], and with darkness we rode to Zeesicx, having ridden twelve miles. February, In the Name of the Lord, 1636, on the land route to Hosacka and below. On Saturday morning, the wind south-southwest, with reasonable weather and a convenient road. We rode through the city of Sulsingau [uncertain], where since I last rode through here, part of the street and next to the Castle had burned down. We rode through a customary broad waterway, passed the high and steep mountain range before Anckabee [uncertain], where we rested. Toward evening we rode through the relay station where the horses were supported by two or three men. We rode to the Vecke Gannija and traveled eleven and a half miles.

text_translated_detailed: Struck from behind by one of our Japanese servants who had gotten drunk and walked into my ribs, which bled considerably. He treated me well, had me bandaged, and we embarked in a vessel to Hosacka [Osaka]. February, In the Name of the Lord, 1636, on the return journey to Fixcando [Firando/Dejima]. On Saturday morning, the wind from the west, with rainy weather. We arrived at the house of the Company's innkeeper, Geobbidon [uncertain]. I received from the Honorable President letters from Tixando [uncertain], stating that he would depart on the twelfth of this month with the fluyt [flute ship] Raxop [uncertain]. With that my entire trade goods were lost. I hired six bankers and the provisions for the journey were made ready by evening. A physician came, rewarded the injected balm which had done much good, and the wound (God be praised, it was not mortal) caused me the most pain internally. On Sunday morning, the wind from the south, with pleasant weather. Since the vessel was not yet ready, I was carried outside the city of Hosacka in a Noximon [a Japanese palanquin]. We visited seven or eight temples with gilded images, went around the great and famous Castle with its moat and stone wall, which was remarkable to see from the outside and very impressive in this land's manner. Toward evening we returned to the lodging, where we were splendidly treated. In the night there was an excessive storm from the west. On Monday morning, the wind from the south, with a storm and rainy weather. We were visited by various merchants, but due to the bad weather we had to remain lying here. On Tuesday morning, the wind from the south, with a light breeze. We loaded my baggage into the Company's vessel that departed downriver. After the meal was done, we took our leave, having been splendidly treated, and sought out the Company's barge with a large vessel. The Nobleman and the interpreter embarked in a cargo barge. We remained lying here that night with good weather.

Ter ander sijde is ons weeder leet geweest te sien hoe dat gem hagenaer druchteloos sonder ijets verricht te hebben weder affe gesonden ende de affdoeninge der saecken vanden gouverneur= andermael uijt gestelt is, wij sullen niet twijffelen maer vastelijck hoopen datse Jmmers Eijntlijck nu met onse persooneele, — verschijninge aldaer door VEcx=te hulpe ende Faveur dercregen werden sall ij sijn met de schenckagie op 25=en dagh vanden sionquats in Osacka wel aengecomen spoeden ons soo seer om bij v Ecx=tie te — verschijnnen als eenichsints mogelijck is, twelck soo tweer — toelaten wil, ongevaerlijck den i1=en a 12=en dach der 2=en maen geschieden sal, den E capiteijn Couckebacker is den 9=en dach der eerste maen Vertroucken, naer welckers vertreck ende affsendinge van alle de scheepen, wij oock eenichsints om boven te comen hebben gewacht, van alle twelcke wij aldaer comende d' Ecx=ne Doecomen onderricht ende contentement sullen doen p= dach der 1=en Maen sijnde van Francoijs Garon aen hollantse stijl 7=m Meert 1636 Natsura Fisenoca misame Jan Firando Ex=tie Waerde Missive dato 1=en dach der 5=en maen is — ons den 3=en dach der 6=en maen met groote vreuchde geworden, waer uijt met een sonderlinge blijschap hebben gesien, het groote Faveur ende de verhelen Eere die sijnne keijserlijcke Maij=t door VEx=re toedoen ende hulpe aen ons ende den gouverneur heeft gelieven te — doen, welcke gave van 200 schuijten
text_translated_detailed: Per the General Comptoir [Office] at Batavia the following ƒ 101217/11/7//— [modern equivalent: guilders, shillings, pence] For as much as the debts listed below, and the remitted cash, as well as other accounts. To the Lord of Tirando, Your Excellency's very pleasant letter of the 28th day of the 12th month [December] to the lord president, was very well delivered to us by the chief merchant Hagenaer on the water between Osaka and Firando, from which we have understood Your Excellency's good disposition with joy, wishing that the same may succeed unchangingly. On the other hand, it has again grieved us to see how that same Hagenaer was sent back fruitlessly without having accomplished anything, and the settlement of the governor's affairs has been postponed once more. We shall not doubt but firmly hope that it will finally now be accomplished with our personal appearance there through Your Excellency's help and favor. We have arrived well with the gifts on the 25th day of the fourth month [April] in Osaka, and we hasten so greatly to appear before Your Excellency as much as is in any way possible, which, if the weather permits, will happen around the 11th or 12th day of the second month [February]. Captain Couckebacker departed on the 9th day of the first month [January], after whose departure and the sending off of all the ships, we have also waited somewhat to come up, of all which upon arriving there we shall inform Your Excellency and provide satisfaction. On the 30th day of the 1st month, being from François Garon in the Dutch style, 7th March 1636, Matsura Fisenoca, my lord, Jan Firando, Your Excellency's worthy letter dated the 1st day of the 5th month [May] was received by us on the 3rd day of the 6th month [June] with great joy, from which with singular gladness we have seen the great favor and the distinguished honor which His Imperial Majesty through Your Excellency's doing and help has been pleased to show to us and the governor, which gift of 200 junks [uncertain: schuyten - possibly a type of vessel or measure]

We send Your Honors this express messenger principally to thank Your Honors kindly, that our servant Itsiseijmon in the past year was so helpful in allowing us to purchase camphor, so that we have obtained our request in part according to our wish. For this reason we beseech the negligence to be taken in good part for this reason. This year we are again desirous to obtain a good quantity of camphor. I should have sent a servant earlier to congratulate Your Excellency, but the many pressing occupations with the arrival of several ships have unfortunately prevented this. I request that Your Excellency be pleased to take this negligence in good part. Letter from the Lord of Firando to His Excellency the President. I write you this letter: that you have sent this merchant here for the release of the governor, has been shown by me to the Council lords. However, since at this time their Highnesses have had so much to do, we have decided not to handle this matter now but after the Sonquats [uncertain: possibly a festival or specific time period]. To keep this merchant here any longer has not been necessary, and on the other hand, since that man was so eager to depart, we have sent him back again. The principal matter shall be told to you entirely by the merchant orally, as time did not permit the matter to be concluded. It has troubled me a thousand times that the matter could not be handled, and it has troubled the merchant no less. But where it cannot be otherwise, patience must be accepted. 12th month, 28th day, being Dutch style, 4th February 1636. From Matsura Fiseno Kami. Furthermore: The Portuguese from Nagasaki have been here for a long time already, February is passing so slowly that I am nearly at a loss. Therefore I advise you, the appointed commissioner, to come as soon as it can possibly be arranged. Letter from the Lord of Firando to Sir François Garon. It has been pleasing that you have so quickly obtained an audience with his Imperial Majesty and license to depart again. The Council lords, not one of them excepted, have accepted the presents, for which I am glad, and I consider your diligence likewise. In the event that with your coming ships there comes any goods or small items, do not put that on the inventory of the cargoes, but let such be sent to me along with a letter.

It has been pleasing that you have obtained audience with His Imperial Majesty so quickly and permission to depart again. The Council members, not one of them excepted, have accepted the presents, for which I am glad, and I consider your joy equally. Letter from the Lord of Firando to the Esteemed President, from the records.

I write you this letter: that you have sent this merchant here for the release of the governor, I have shown to the Council members. From Matsura Fishenno Camij

Letter from the Lord of Firando to Sir François Garon.
