We [on the] 28th of August for the General Comptoir in Batavia, the following:

101217/11/7

As far as the debts listed below and the remittances sent, as well as other accounts [are concerned].

Letter from the Lord of Firando.

I send you this letter. I believe that by this time your first ships will already have arrived there. The Council members are instructed that the trade of the 20 persons and all their daily dealings in the merchandise has proceeded very irregularly and not as it should. I have taken responsibility for this and have brought it so far that the 20 persons are permitted to trade with Your Excellency once more. However, I advise you and say for your benefit that you should set aside these aforementioned 20 persons exclusively for this year somewhat from your hand, and not use them through other coming merchants. Instruct these people, for on my part it is not fitting to do such a thing, and say that they shall remain somewhat behind this year and shall not be too eager to buy much, which shall benefit them hereafter and better accountability. Be watchful of that.

Just as I have written to you before, that in case any provisions come with your ships and are demanded by the governors of Nagasaki, you shall answer them that Matsura Teckeno camij has strictly charged you to deliver to no one other than him that which might be of service to His Majesty or the great [uncertain: possibly "great lord" or "great service"]. The price of your silver is also charged this year to be the same as that which shall be agreed upon in Nagasaki. That which you have further to request has been requested by me from the Council members. When I receive approval, I shall send it to you with the first opportunity. If any living creatures come, say that they have come as gifts to me so that I may present them again to His Majesty's gentlemen.

Understood. Firando, received 5th month, 9th day, being Dutch style, 12th of June, year 1636.

text_original: aende Ed Heer generael Anthonio van diemen Ede Manhafte weel wijse Voorsinnige en zeer discreten heer VEd Missive vanden 29=en december p=r t' schip de galiasse als mede van 19=en Januarij met t' Jacht Texel, zijn ons op 21=en februarij p=r de galias, en op 3=en Maert, met t' Jacht Texel successivelijck toe gecomen op welcke wij door de cortheit des tijts, naer onse Regeerte, met connen Antwoorden, Maer zullen het selve. tot de naeste Besendinghe. Moeten lent stellen op welcke versoecke l'Ed ten goede gelieft te nemen alsoo het niet door naerlaeticheijt maer door gebreck des tijts geschiet, de toegesonden cargasoenen, hebbe naer Ontfanck desselffs, de Molucos, voor laeten Belasten Ende aent generael goet doen, de galiasse, Is int herwarts comen, Jnde straet van Bouten aen gront geraeckt geweest, soo dat genootsaeckt geweest zijn om daer wederom van te comen, eenighe rijs overboort te werpen, waerover op de toegesonde. 46" lasten rijs 8 te cort comen, alsmede 2. leggers aracq die heel leedich bevonden hebben. text_translated_detailed: To the Esteemed Lord General Antonio van Diemen [Antonio van Diemen], the Valiant, Wise, Prudent and most Discreet Lord. Your Esteemed Missive of the 29th of December last by the ship the Galeas, as well as of the 19th of January by the Yacht Texel, came to us successively on the 21st of February by the Galeas, and on the 3rd of March by the Yacht Texel. On account of the shortness of time, according to our capacity, we have not been able to answer in accordance with our governance, but we shall have to defer the same until the next dispatch. We request that Your Esteemed will take this kindly, since it has occurred not through negligence but through lack of time. The cargoes that were sent, after we received them, we had loaded for the Moluccas and delivered to the general good. The Galeas, on the return journey, ran aground in the Strait of Banten, so that we were forced to come off from there again, throwing some rice overboard, on account of which from the 46 [lasts: modern equivalent: approximately 80-100 tons] of rice sent, we came up 8 short, as well as 2 barrels of arrack [a type of distilled spirit] which we found completely empty. As for Citchil Grontale, the present King of Tidore, we can understand and learn nothing other than that he is entirely devoted to Spain. However, now with the arrival of Spanish reinforcements, the new governor does not seem to us to be very satisfied, according to what we are informed, because the Tidorese had deposed their subordinate king and placed Grontale in his place, whom he said was bound in too great friendship with the Ternatan, which worked to the detriment and contempt of their previously undertaken design, as he now well perceives, saying furthermore that if the subordinate King Citchil Narolamme had remained in the government, affairs there would have found themselves in better condition. He showed himself entirely discontented about this, but what shall we write to you with certainty about it? The reports and rumors are so many and varied that no reliance can be placed upon them. As far as concerns the old King of Tidore, Citchil Naro Lammo, he is with the Ternatan King and the great one here in low esteem, and he himself leads a foul and shameful life, so that recently three women who had been debauched by him have been put to death, namely one of the King's concubines, one of the King of Gilolo, and one of our other great ones. This was a very great cause of disturbance in his life. The King of Ternate came to us in the castle and sought our council in this matter, how he should deal with the Tidore King in this situation. As we could understand, His Majesty was inclined to put him to death, but we have with many reasons and good counsel held back the same and brought matters to such a point that the King did not proceed with his intention.

text_original: 3R13 Aende Edle Generael Anthonio van diemen Edele Manhafte wel wijse Voorsinghe en heer discrete heer — Wijn heere onse Jonghsten aen VEEd is geweest van dato 20=en Maert over Amboina waer bij VEEd wel sult hebben verstaen. de Behouden over compste van schepen de galiasse op 21 februarij en Texel op den 3=en Maert passado die wij vertrouwen VEd voor den ontfanck deser wel sal ter handt gecomen sijn waer van hier neffens Copie is gaende VEd sal daermede wel hebben beooght, het gepasseerde Inde quartieren van Molnco, t' sedert onse aencompste aldaer s. T'seedert zijn ons jn Molnco op 17e April over Amboina behouden toe gecomen de Jachten tergoes Ende Zeeburch benevens v Ed Aengenamen van 19=en februarij waermede van Batavia ons zijn toegesonde 1700 Balen Japansen. Rijs, Ende 300 van Amboina maeckende t' samen 2000 halen wij hebben conform factuire de Molus daer vooren belast, en aen t' generael, laeten goet doen, Except dat bij den Rijs wtt de galiaste acht en wit Texel 6½ lasten te cort compt Maeckende t'samen 14½ lasten, het is veel op het sober ons voor dees tijt toe gesonden, bij het Cargasoen ons met het Jacht tergoes toegecomen wert mede gemist gel. mede meede bij factuire ende Conosement blijckt, een calle met zyde stoffen genombert 113. die niet en hebbe gecregh wij hebben den schipper Ende Coopman daer over aengesprock die seggen dat ditto Casse niet en hebben Ontfangh noch int schip en is geweest, gelijk vlEd bij nevens gaende acte sult. connen beooghen Bij onse voorige Missive als mede copie van Resolutie heeft VEEd connen verstaen wat redenen ons hebben beweght de schepen de galias en Texel op te houden en niet volgens dordere van VEEd naer Amboina gesonden en sijn, het welck wij oock p=r Expresse praeuw aen heere
text_translated_detailed: To the Noble General Antonio van Diemen [António van Diemen], Noble, Valiant, Wise, Provident, and most Discreet Lord. Our letter to Your Excellency is of the twentieth of March via Amboina, whereby Your Excellency shall well have understood the safe arrival of the ships the Galias on the twenty-first of February and Texel on the third of March past, which we trust shall have come to Your Excellency's hand before the receipt of this, of which a copy is enclosed herewith. Your Excellency shall thereby well have observed what has transpired in the quarters of the Moluccas since our arrival there. Since then, on the seventeenth of April, there have arrived to us in the Moluccas via Amboina the yachts Tergoes and Zeeburch, together with Your Excellency's esteemed letter of the nineteenth of February, with which from Batavia there have been sent to us 1700 bales of Japanese rice and 300 from Amboina, making together 2000 bales, which we have according to invoice charged to the Moluccas and have had accounted for to the General, except that with the rice from the Galias eight and from the Texel six and a half [modern equivalent: lasts/cargo units] come short, making together fourteen and a half lasts. It is much less than what was sent to us for the present time. With the cargo that came to us with the yacht Tergoes, there was also missed, as likewise appears from the invoice and bill of lading, a case with silk fabrics numbered 113, which we have not received. We have spoken to the skipper and merchant about this, who say that said case they have not received, nor has it been in the ship, as Your Excellency shall be able to observe from the enclosed act. By our previous missive as well as copy of the resolution, Your Excellency could understand what reasons have moved us to hold the ships the Galias and Texel and not to send them to Amboina according to Your Excellency's order, which we have also by express prau advised to the Lord

text_translated_detailed: The merchant was spoken to about this, and they say that the aforementioned cash was neither received nor was it ever on the ship, as you will be able to observe from the attached document. Through our previous letter and also a copy of the resolution, you will have been able to understand what reasons moved us to detain the ships the Galias and Texel and not to send them to Amboina according to your orders. We have also advised the Governor and the Council in Amboina of this by express prau, and we requested that they be pleased to assist us in this situation with their advice as to how we should proceed with the aforementioned ships—whether it would be advisable to send them as soon as the Spanish force had wholly or partly departed, with the ready cloves that were approximately seven hundred bahars [modern equivalent: approximately 700 bahars, a unit of weight], as quickly as possible to Batavia so that they could be further used there by you, or whether it would be better to dispatch the said ships directly from here to Taiwan, so that the Company's excellent trade there would not be neglected due to a lack of ships. Following this, on the night of May [date], the ship Wassenaer and the yacht P. Waterloose arrived here from Amboina. After the arrival of the aforementioned ship and yacht, I spoke with Commander Theunis Jacobsz Engelsz and also gave you the instruction for the exploit for which the ships Wassenaer, the Galias, and Texel were ordered. This was opened and examined, and its contents—we would have gladly followed it, but the situation in the Moluccas did not permit it at this time. We therefore convened the Council and gave them consideration as to how we should regulate ourselves in this situation. On the one hand, seeing the Spanish force, and on the other hand, the bad conduct and false dealings of Ternate, in whom we could not place our trust, but we had all the more reason to see, as it had shortly become clear from the Spaniard himself, what lay hidden in the heart of this treacherous King Hamza. A few days ago, namely on the 29th of March, all the Singadias, Chimelahas, and the Sousives appeared before us at the Castle on behalf of the King, and they sought with many frivolous reasons to persuade us to allow them to build a fortress in their quarter so that in time of need or in case of an enemy attack they could secure their wives and children there. They said that it was well known to us how strong the Spaniard had become here in the Moluccas, and furthermore that the war with the Tidorese had already begun and was also fierce, and that it therefore behooved them to attend to the protection of their wives and children. However, to all their proposals and unreasonable requests, we answered nothing other than that we would not permit anyone to build any fortress or stronghold near our Castle, but would forbid the same with weapons. Whereupon they again said that they intended to proceed with it, and if the work was already done and we did not like it, they could then have it torn down again.

Upon this, after much and various deliberation and debate, it was unanimously decided to be good that the ships Wassenaar, Texel, and the galley here in Moluco should remain until the end of May, and if the Spaniard had still not departed by then, we would further resolve what would be most serviceable and expedient for the general Company. Above all, careful attention was paid to the trade in China, so that the Company might suffer no damage there through lack of ships. The insight of ourselves and the Council, by which we came to this resolution, was firstly because the ships were destined for an exploit which was uncertain whether anything more advantageous would be brought about through it or not. Secondly, because time had progressed so far that to execute the design Your Excellency had charged us with would have been too late. We and the Council deemed it most necessary to prevent the danger that lay before us and was seen with our own eyes, rather than to undertake a doubtful matter at hand, the outcome of which would be entirely uncertain.

text_translated_detailed: As we trust that his person in this situation and time in the quarters of Amboina [Ambon] or Ceram might accomplish something good for the Company's interests, and the placate [edict] regarding the making of testaments have been followed, we have had it published by order and posted in the proper place. Likewise, all upper and lower merchants together with the assistants, or all those who are qualified to write testaments, have been warned that they must regulate themselves according to the placate so that we would keep them free from damage. The sick-comforter of the yacht Texel, named Jan de Lange, has been here prosecuted by the fiscal regarding the sale of some amphioen [a type of cloth or goods] amounting to 60 rixdollars [modern equivalent: a substantial sum]. This amphioen was sold to the King of Hamspia, and when he wished to pay the same to the aforementioned de Lange with crowns and double stuivers [modern equivalent: small coins], it was refused by him, saying that he wished to be paid with Spanish money. Whereupon the King requested of us that we would be pleased to accommodate him with 100 rixdollars in Spanish currency, as the people of the ships would not accept Dutch money. To make this request to us came the King's Turtullus with some people from Macquan [Makian], who then had quite a bit to say. He said that we held ourselves so poorly satisfied, that Dutch money was refused at Macquan, in which they said they had no wrong, as they saw and found that the Netherlanders would not accept the same. Wherefore they had to reward the Dutch money not particularly. We asked them whether they would accept Coupans or crowns in the shop or the warehouse, and they would get everything that pleased them. They said yes, but added to that the Dutch money was desired by no one except only by us, and also that it was not suitable to have anything of theirs made from it. And when they then came to our merchants to exchange some Holland money for you, they sent them away, saying there was no Spanish money at the Comptoirs [trading posts], with this demand of the Spanish and the refusal of Dutch money we have gotten much trouble on our hands, so that it is to be feared that still the Ternate people or the Macquan people will not want to accept Dutch money anymore. These Roven [uncertain: possibly a name or term] named 60 rixdollars from Jan de Lange have been confiscated by the Council and forfeited to the profit of the Company and for the benefit of the fiscal. Per advice—the skipper of the ship Tertholen [Tertholen], Jan Phlipsz [Philippsz], whose contracted time having fully expired, has again accepted the nova [renewal of contract] for the period of three years following in succession to serve in his previous capacity under improved treatment of 68 to eighty-five guilders per month. The Gougoe answered to this that the King was ashamed to appear before us, and that for reasons he had made us real and great promises to undertake war against the Tidorese, and that upon all his promises, nothing had followed thus far, saying this alone was the reason that held the King back from coming to us. With the Colano Noffagnaris we had many reasons on this matter as well, namely regarding this aversion, both on their part and on the King's part, which they answered us by saying that since the killing of the sengadja of Gammacnorra and his son, as well as the deposition of the sengadja of Guofficqia, great fear had come upon them, in that they saw that if anyone of theirs sought the company of Netherlanders somewhat more than the King approved, they would be held suspect and hated, whereby they could expect nothing other than death, or at the very least their ruin and destruction, saying this alone was the reason that they showed themselves so strangely and aversely to us. It is not without reason that these people held themselves somewhat strange from us, for when the matters, in the time of the Lord Governor Loodensteijn, were brought so far by ours that one would have removed King Hampsia from power and deposed him from the Crown, and everything was prepared for this so that one would proceed with the work, then the Governor drew back and held with the King's party, which then did not go well for the heads who had taken this matter in hand, as is evident from what happened to the sengadja of Gammacnorra, his son, and those of Guofficqia. text_translated_detailed: And so with Thoolen and Zeeburch [Ternate] departing for that place on the 12th of July, the ship Thoolen would remain ahead in the strait, so that while we would provision Batsian [Bacan] with Zeeburch, we would procure there wood for beams and spars for the projected redoubt on Cabalola. To this he had us answer through the interpreter that this was beyond his expectation, as he had now planned to make an expedition to Tidore and to show that he was serious about it, in order to fulfill the desire of Your Excellency and to follow our good counsel in this matter. Furthermore, he said he would first come to us to speak of this. But since we were to board on the morning of the 12th, the King appeared at us in the Castle, with whom we spoke for some time. text_translated_detailed: At the Company's office of this monsoon we received over forty [uncertain: Bhaeren] of pure cloves, dry and well conditioned. It would be desirable if one could bring those from Machan to do the same, so that their cloves would likewise be delivered, for which we know no counsel to persuade them to do so. Tidore lies too near. This King of Batsjan shows himself quite unfriendly and an enemy of King Hampsia, saying that he is a Spanish-oriented person who is devoted to the Spaniard with heart and soul. He has told us that he certainly knows and is well aware that the aforementioned Ternate King has been in negotiations with the Macassar for some time, and that he does not doubt that an accord has been struck. Furthermore, that they are planning to join their forces in general, both the Tidorees and several others with one another, to ally with the Spaniard and thus to fall upon us with force and drive us out of the Moluccas and Amboina. And this done, the Spaniard would also receive a portion, whereby they then thought they knew counsel to be able to conduct their trade freely and unhindered with the Javanese, Malays, and others (as in olden times). We said to the King of Batsjan that we well believed that this might be their will and intention, but to carry the same out, there is something more than mere talk or opinion required. These are Moorish rumors, upon which mostly little comes to pass. Experience will best make their intention known to us. In our previous letter we have written to Your Excellency how the King of Batsjan had requested of us that he, according to the contracts, would likewise be allowed to enjoy such toll and rights on the cloves as the King of Ternate was receiving. Your Excellency would please give us orders with the first opportunity on how we should regulate ourselves in this matter. What the Batsjan King has requested is mostly in conformity with the Company contracts, whereby he is also recognized as a confederate, mostly in the same form as the Ternate King. After we had conducted the Company's affairs in Batsjan, we departed from there and proceeded further to Machan, where we arrived well on the 4th of July, finding there the Gougoe who brought the corregidor and the people of Machan firmly together. Everything was arranged as if one had completely destroyed the Tidorees. The Gougoe came aboard to us and told us that now almost everything was ready to depart from there with the honey with us to Malaya. To this we answered that we still had well five or six days of work there to conduct some affairs for the Company, to which he said that this was fine, so that then both could be ready at the same time. We would have begun to believe by chance that the Ternate King was serious about the matter. Meanwhile, while we lay at Machan, the Gougoe came to us daily, but no one from the authorities of Machan appeared. He told us that King Hampsia on his departure

And this yacht comes to Your Excellency as well, a certain Jan Argell, an Englishman—formerly a ensign [military rank] on Batsjan, a great drunkard. And since we, while being there, had spoken to him somewhat harshly about his disorderly conduct, and threatened him with dismissal, and giving orders to the under-merchant there that if the aforementioned ensign Jan Argell continued in his old debauchery and did not conduct himself as an honorable soldier ought to do, that we would in such a case suspend him from his position and salary, and send him to us at the first opportunity. So it happened that after our departure, the aforementioned Jan Argell, in the evening, after the word had been brought back to the merchant, and he came to the bulwark, said to the corporal and others: "I will not bring it to the merchant anymore," and thus went to his quarters, shut the door, and hanged himself. Now hanging between heaven and earth, he began to sigh and groan greatly, which was heard by the soldiers on the bulwark. In such a way that the corporal and others, having run to open the door of the quarters, found him as described before, and hastily cut him down, so that he remained alive. We could find nothing otherwise than that this deed was carried out by him with premeditation, in order thereby to frighten the under-merchant, so that he would let him continue in his debauchery without daring to punish him further. Thus he deceived himself. As soon as this matter was reported to us by the under-merchant, we had him removed from Batsjan and brought to Malaya [Ambon], where, having arrived, we had him addressed by the fiscal [legal officer], and after we had obtained good knowledge of everything and heard his own confession, he was by us and the council dismissed from his office and position, and deemed unworthy to be employed by the Honored Company in any service further. Item, that he should be sent from here without salary or wages to Batavia, as Your Excellency will be pleased to examine by the accompanying copy of the sentence and other documents. There has also come to us here from Batavia a certain Claes van Bengale, who says he served the Honored Company as a soldier in Banda. And since he appeared here in the Moluccas without order or consent, we have had him put in chains, to work therein as long as we shall receive advice from Batavia regarding his life and conduct.

text_translated_detailed: This astonished us greatly, as nothing of this sort had ever been requested before, and since this matter was of such weight and consequence, it could not be decided by us but had to be decided by Your Excellency in Batavia, as it concerned not only the Honored Company but also the inhabitants of Batchian. When they replied to this, we said that we had sufficient command, power, and authority to grant such a thing, and that previously we had always been accustomed to settle such matters, with requests for provisions and negotiations, as they had requested, and we had been obliged to comply, just as we had also assisted them with a ship to Papua, which still happens daily. And when their request was not taken into consideration by us and was not granted, they threatened not to pluck any more cloves, moreover making light of whether we would abandon our fort or not. In this way we never satisfied them with fine words alone, and they had always seen the effects of our promises. But the delay in the ship going to Lapoes arose solely from the consideration which Your Excellency had taken, through the six Dutch persons who, several years ago, together with a party of Batchianers, went on an expedition in the year 1632 and did not return. Furthermore, if Your Excellency resolved to abandon the fort, they had firmly to believe that this would bring them advantage, and that instead of their arrogant demands, they ought to consider what excessive great costs and burdens the Honored Company had borne to protect them, and still bears daily. When our reasonable answer, that we would write in their favor, was well received, and they should remain content. After which we likewise declared that on the said expedition not only our aforementioned persons but also part of the principal men of Batchian were killed, and that our men were seduced by the good appearance of obtaining booty from outside.

text_translated_detailed: The King sent word through his scribe, which we found strange, that His Majesty had not appeared before us in person, but rather the authorities of Makian had sent someone who came to us with contrived excuses and made our heads hot with talk, and upon whose request no determination could be made except in the presence of the aforementioned His Majesty. We requested that it please him to appear before us the next day, as we had various matters to conduct with him. Accordingly, on the following day, the aforementioned Jurtullus [uncertain: title or name] appeared with an envoy, who declared that His Majesty of Ternate, after having received the report from what had transpired the day before, had instructed them to answer us that if the matter of those from Makian, the occasion of war, or the kingdom of Ternate had been affected, he would have appeared before us in person. But since it concerned only those of Makian in particular, in order to remove all suspicion from the aforementioned authorities, he had refrained from doing so. Moreover, since the cloves were theirs, after they had brought the toll, they could sell them according to their pleasure and at whatever high price they themselves thought fit. And that there were various other matters that had kept him from coming above. The aforementioned scribe also declared how those of Makian had intended to forbid the Dutch currency, under penalty of a fine and corporal punishment, but that the delivery of cloves would begin. Were these not remarkable excuses from the King for why he had absented himself? We answered the Jurtullus thereupon that we could not accept the King's excuse, as it contradicted all reason, and that the King ought to be ashamed to send us such an answer. And because such acts were entirely intolerable, the aforementioned King of Gilolo and Chitchil Japon requested that they might avenge this with swords, for which purpose the previous evening he had stood ready in his house to do so, as reparation had been made, but was held back by him until such time as he would have spoken with us about this, since he did not wish to begin the same without our knowledge. We answered his Majesty upon this that nothing strengthens the conduct of great princes as much as the lord's wisdom tempered with grace and gentleness, and that through no virtue did they come closer to the Divine Nature than in forgiving those who had transgressed. Thus concluding that if the aforementioned King of Tidore were to have him killed, it would be regarded by the surrounding peoples as tyranny. Therefore, in our judgment it was best that he be sent elsewhere, to one place or another to dwell. We therefore gave him serious warning that he must desist from such matters, or if anything should come to pass over this, he would have to bear the punishment of the same upon his head, and would be innocent of it if he wished to be. This counsel also seemed best to the Council, and they promised us they would follow the same. The next day the King of Gilolo and Chitchil Japon came with an agreed-upon messenger.

text_translated_detailed: He set the 18th of March following, when King Hampsia appeared with few of his orangkais [court officials] at our Castle, who after some friendly discourse had taken place on both sides declared that he had knowledge and information that the Tidorese and Spaniard a few days before had taken it upon themselves to make war on him, whereupon he began to come to the content of Your Excellency's Letter, saying that the same was set forth very hard and sharp against him, and in length and breadth we presented his daily procedures and intolerable acts, and that nothing other than what was right and proper (and all of which we had also previously presented to him) was inserted, comprised, and understood in the same, together with Your Excellency's true meaning and intention. Furthermore, he should firmly trust that the content of the same was the Resolution of Your Excellency and the Gentlemen Council of the Indies in Batavia, and if he persevered in his old harmful opinions, he should expect no more favor, help, or assistance from Your Excellency, but the contrary would follow, since we found the Company's state in Molucca to be such that with God's help it was sufficiently steadfast to protect against all their evil practices, the cunning of the Tidorese, and the deception and falsity of the Spaniards, to maintain and preserve our justice. This being thus presented to him, we saw clearly a remarkable change in his manner and bearing, lowering his head, remaining seated as one to whom something burdensome comes or who is troubled, without answer. In this way, proceeding further, we declared to him that now was the time to attend to the preservation of his kingdom and state, and that the delay must now once and for all be ended, and he should follow our good counsel, with which Your Excellency and the Gentlemen Council of the Indies in Batavia would give singular good satisfaction and contentment,

text_translated_detailed: 3R225 A DECLARATION Explanation of a certain Bastian Leuwa, born in Manila, who came this year with the Spanish reinforcement from there and now in the Moluccas came over to us at Malaya from Gammalamma. This person had spent two years consecutively with the ships from Manila in Nueva España or Acapulco. This Bastian Leuwa we summoned to us, and interrogated him regarding all the circumstances of the voyage from Manila to Nueva España. First, in what month these ships depart from Manila and how long they are on the voyage before arriving in Acapulco; secondly, when these ships have taken on the silver in Nueva España, for how long they then depart again from there to Manila, and how long they are on that same voyage before arriving there; also what quantity of silver or eight-real pieces they bring with them. He says that the ships which depart from Manila toward Nueva España or Acapulco set sail in the month of July, between the 10th and 25th, and take five months and 25 days before arriving in Nueva España, or also twelve, six months, and more, depending on how well the ships are sailed. And when they have taken on the silver in Acapulco, they depart from there in the month of March between the 5th and 15th without delaying any longer, being then underway before passing the Ladrone Islands between 40 and 50 days, sometimes 42 3/4" and 45 days but at the longest not more than 50. And then further from the Ladrones to Cape del Espíritu Santo or the Bocadera they take 20", 21", or "22" days, so that they always pass through the Embocadero in the month of May or come through, so that the arrival of the ships from Nueva España in Manila is always around Saint John's Day, sometimes
